articles.title: 13 km inside Lebanon: How IDF commandos seized Hezbollah stronghold Khiam in 36 hours
articles.body:
Nearly two years after the battle, the IDF has revealed details of one of Maglan’s most significant operations during the Northern Arrows campaign, when commandos advanced some 13 kilometers (8 miles) into southern Lebanon and fought their way through Hezbollah’s defenses in Khiam.
According to the military account, Maglan forces dismantled successive Hezbollah defensive and command positions and gained control of the town in less than two days.
“You don’t forget the cold of November nights in Lebanon, no matter how much time passes, even if you’re in the commandos,” recalled Lt. Col. Z., who commanded Maglan at the time.
“It was freezing,” he said. “I grew up on the ethos that you don’t fight in Lebanon during the winter because the conditions are simply too difficult. But during Northern Arrows, we had to reach Khiam at exactly that time.”
Maglan’s mission was to take control of the northern part of the town, neutralize Hezbollah command centers there and eliminate anti-tank capabilities that threatened Metula, roughly 13 kilometers to the south.
It was the unit’s final battle of the campaign after dozens of special operations.
“We came into it as veterans of three battles, but this one was different from all the others,” Z. said. “It combined depth with the front line.”
Maglan’s ‘secret sauce’
Lt. Col. A., a reservist who commanded Maglan’s detection-and-strike element, said the unit was selected because the mission required a combination of stealth, intelligence gathering, special operations and maneuver warfare.
“Traditionally, we stand on three legs: detection and strike, special operations and maneuver,” he said. “Khiam is a complex target at tactical depth that has to be reached covertly. Only when you use all the components correctly and add the ‘secret sauce’ does all the magic come together.”
The detection-and-strike method, he explained, allows the same force that identifies an enemy to close the targeting cycle within seconds.
“It is a technique that lets us actively expose the enemy,” A. said. “The same team discovers the terrorists and closes the circle on them within seconds, with zero bureaucracy.”
The capability began developing inside the unit in the 1990s during operations including Grapes of Wrath and Accountability, relying on close coordination with the Israeli Air Force and advanced technology.
“It becomes part of your soul, hunting the enemy,” A. said. “It requires a rare combination of patience, terrain analysis, understanding and the fusion of intelligence.”
Four days of preparation around Khiam
For the troops who entered Lebanon, the depth of the operation was evident almost immediately.
“We hadn’t been out of regular service for very long when we were called up to Lebanon,” recalled Staff Sgt. G., a reservist in one of the teams. “We put on our gear, waited for the vehicles and crossed the border. It took 40 minutes to reach the drop-off point. I remember us looking at each other and saying, ‘Wow, we’ve gone really deep.’”
The area had proved difficult for the IDF during the Second Lebanon War. This time, commanders chose a different approach: drive as far as the terrain allowed and then continue on foot across the hills and mountains, with the goal of reaching northern Khiam in a single night.
Khiam lies between two mountain ridges, and at the time of the operation the surrounding areas were under Hezbollah control, according to the IDF.
“To deal with that, we deployed teams at different ranges on the hills around the town four days before the first ground entry,” Z. said.
After what G. described as an hours-long climb, the teams reached their positions and divided responsibilities.
“We stopped at one point and began observing,” he recalled. “I sat with the Negev machine gun on my knee and noticed a wooded hill about 70 meters away.”
His squad commander told him another Israeli force was positioned behind the trees and that nobody should be moving between the two positions.
“As soon as he finished speaking, I saw three figures in the background,” G. said. “They were walking strangely and carrying weapons. There was no room for doubt. I cocked the Negev and opened fire.”
Other troops immediately joined the firefight.
“There was a special synchronization between us. We just did what we had practiced,” he said. “I remember the guys shouting throughout the encounter until we killed the other two as well.”
Only the next morning did he realize how close the Hezbollah terrorists had been.
“We passed the place where the encounter happened and suddenly understood that it hadn’t been anywhere near 70 meters,” he said. “They had been seven to 10 meters away from us, and even so we managed to take control of the situation very quickly.”
The first 36 hours
For Maglan’s commanders, the central challenge was turning intelligence collected before the operation into an accurate battlefield picture while events unfolded.
“You are constantly racing against time to locate and eliminate the right terrorist cell,” Z. said.
The IDF’s 7th Armored Brigade approached from the south, while commando forces operated from the north and west, supported by intelligence collection at both close and long range.
A. recalled one incident in which several Hezbollah terrorists were spotted fleeing from Khiam’s old quarter toward a nearby wadi.
“One of our forces locked onto them and eliminated them,” he said. “We could have said, ‘Mission accomplished, we’re done here.’ But what did the team do? We redeployed and concentrated effort on that point because the indication was correct. We waited, more terrorists appeared, we engaged them and they were eliminated.”
According to Z., Hezbollah repeatedly attempted to ambush the advancing troops but instead found its own forces being attacked.
“The enemy tries to surprise you, but finds itself surprised instead, and within 36 hours from the start of the battle it is defeated,” he said.
“They did not expect to encounter a force moving that sharply and precisely. We simply waited for the terrorists to make a mistake and attacked them with missiles, drones and additional capabilities until most of the local command chain had been eliminated.”
For A., the operation represented the culmination of decades of experience.
“Twenty-five years led me to this battle,” he joked. “When it ended, I said, ‘That’s it, I’m retiring at the top.’”
He said individual soldiers rarely grasp the full scale of an operation while it is underway.
“One soldier fired 12 mortar rounds, another encountered a terrorist face to face and a third was clearing houses in the town,” he said. “Only when they hear the full picture do they fall silent and understand the power of what they accomplished, step by step.”

articles.title: Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions blocked by a second judge – US politics live
articles.body:
Trump and Republican allies rail against AI controls despite growing calls for more checks – live
Trump dismisses threat of AI as a ‘hoax’ after tech CEOs call for slowing pace of development; Republican House speaker says he will meet with AI execs ‘soon’ alongside president
Trump claims 'sick conspiracy' over calls for more guardrails on AI companies
Donald Trump has claimed there is a “SICK conspiracy” against artificial intelligence and data centers in response to the growing calls for greater checks on AI development.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on Truth Social, insisting that the administration has stopped leaders of AI companies from “doing bad, or potentially bad” things. However, he didn’t point to any concrete examples for how he has curbed possible abuse or malfeasance in the industry.
The president said over the weekend that the AI arms race is of the utmost importance for US national security. “Whoever wins AI wins,” he told reporters on a visit to Ireland, before repeating it on social media today. Trump also chided Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, who we noted earlier has called to slow down AI’s advancement to ensure public safety. This comes after company whistleblowers claimed that the technology has the potential to “kill all of humanity” within the decade.
Trump accused Amodei of “now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’”, and claimed that the administration has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies”.
The president added:
There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China … We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!
Some more context following the news that Mike Johnson and DonaldTrump are set to meet with AI company executives by the end of this week or early next.
Trump met privately with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backstage at the Republican midterm convention last week, according to MS Now.
Citing three people familiar with the matter, Altman met with the president on Thursday, just days after Jacob Coxon – a former researcher for Anthropic and OpenAI said that “neither company was acting responsibly”, as the technology continued to develop rapidly.
According to one of MS Now’s sources, Altman requested the meeting with the president, which was reportedly centered on artificial intelligence and its growing power. Altman was also one of the CEOs who spoke out about the need for increased guardrails.
Johnson says he will meet with AI execs 'soon' alongside Trump
House speaker Mike Johnson told reporters on Capitol Hill that the White House will schedule a meeting with artificial intelligence executives and company CEOs “soon”.
“I think either end of this week or early next week. But wait and see,” he told reporters.
The speaker didn’t say whether Congress would try and rush through any legislation to curb AI development this week, before House lawmakers head out of Washington to continue campaigning ahead of the November midterms. However, Johnson confirmed that the Ratepayer Protection Act – a piece of legislation that would require tech companies to cover the costs associated with datacenters – will head to the House floor this week. The speaker said that he supported the bill.
On Sunday, Johnson said it was up to tech companies, not Congress, to guarantee the safety of their artificial intelligence products. However, on the Hill today, he seemed to say that the legislative branch could have “a role” moving forward, but did not want to act “irrationally or haphazardly”.
“The reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and hyper-regulation. If you do that, then you lose your edge, and that is a national security concern for the American people,” he said.
Trump 'open to' talks with Iran, insists that countries should reimburse US for oil arriving through strait of Hormuz
On Truth Social, Donald Trump also claimed that Iran wants to make a deal “quickly and badly”, and that while the US president will “determine” whether to engage, the US is “open to” the “concept”.
This comes after scheduled talks between Gulf states and Iran about the future control of the strait of Hormuz, were postponed today.
Earlier, Trump insisted that other countries who have benefited from oil that has arrived through the vital passageway should ultimately reimburse the US.
“The Countries of the World, which have been no help to us whatsoever, should, and will, reimburse the United States of America when this SCAM Confligration is all over,” Trump said. “We are doing it much more for others, than we are for ourselves, and we have been for Generations!”
The president has claimed that the “only reason” that there has been such consternation about increased guardrails on artificial intelligence is because the US is “leading” development of new technology. “Don’t kill the Golden Goose!” Trump warned on Truth Social.
However, the recent pushback, including from leading AI company CEOs has been in response to employees who have warned of irresponsible and “reckless” growth in the space, which – they argue – is threatening humanity.
Alligator Alcatraz held detainees in cages the size of phone booths, DHS watchdog says
Richard Luscombe
Before the facility was shuttered, detainees at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” federal immigration jail were frequently locked in outside metal cages no bigger than a phone booth, according to a damning government watchdog report that said the practice “does not align with standards for humane treatment”.
The findings from the office of the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) were published on its website – and offer rare criticism of the Trump administration by one of its own agencies.
The report also provides the first official confirmation that guards repeatedly used the highly restrictive cages on detainees in direct contravention of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rules.
In December, the Guardian was the first to report an Amnesty International dossier detailing multiple alleged human rights abuses at the controversial camp in the remote Florida Everglades, including how people were regularly shackled outside in metal cages for hours as well as exposed to brutal heat, sunshine and swarms of mosquitoes.
At the time, a spokesperson for Ron DeSantis, the Republican Florida governor whose administration ran Alligator Alcatraz on behalf of the federal government, dismissed the claims now confirmed by the DHS report as “fabrications” – and the Amnesty report as “a politically motivated attack”.
The same spokesperson did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on Monday.
The notorious immigration jail closed in June after a year of operation during which DeSantis boasted of detaining and deporting more than 21,000 immigrants. Officials cited the risk of holding detainees in tents during hurricane season for the closure.
Further to his earlier post dismissing grave calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”, Donald Trump continued to defend the growth of AI and spread of data centers as going to be “the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History — Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet.”
He wrote on Truth Social:
Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy? AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX, no different from RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA — UKRAINE, UKRAINE, UKRAINE — IMPEACHMENT HOAX #1 — IMPEACHMENT HOAX #2 — and all of the other HOAXES and SCAMS that America was forced to endure through the Destructionists’ and Deviants’ foul play and illegal conduct. President Xi, of China, just announced that China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future. Google has recently stated that they want to build a massive Plant in Finland, all because they are finding permitting too difficult in the United States. I am not happy about this, and want them to change their thinking. AI, and Data Centers, will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History — Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet. It will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP!
AI-linked stocks tumbled this morning after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.
Trump again touts $5,000 payments if GOP retains control of Congress
Donald Trump is still touting his pledge to give a “Trump dividend” of $5,000 to every adult US citizen if Republicans win November’s midterm elections.
The pledge has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery, with a huge question mark still hanging over its legality - not to mention it comes at a time of extreme concern over the national debt, which exceeded $40tn for the first time last month.
He posted about it again just now on Truth Social:
The $5,000 Trump Dividend, to be given to all Adults in the United States due to the fact that our Country is taking in Trillions of Dollars of Economic Development, Investment, and Pure SUCCESS, is being criticized by “Dumocrats” who are hoping that it never happens — But it will! As an example, the Dumocrats said THE GREAT BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL, one of the largest ever approved by Congress, or signed into Law by a President happened, despite the Dumocrats saying it would be impossible to get approved — Or the Gift of $1776 that I gave last year to our Military, was an almost guaranteed Non Starter, everyone said it could not be done, but it was, our Military Patriots got the money, and loved it. When I say something, I mean it! The $5,000 Dividend will happen because the People of our Country deserve it. VOTE REPUBLICAN — MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!
Senate Republicans release new crypto bill text ahead of critical Tuesday vote
Senate Republicans have released a revised draft of major cryptocurrency legislation which they said addressed Democrats’ concerns over ethics provisions, as well as banking industry concerns that the bill could hurt lending, ahead of a key vote tomorrow.
The Clarity Act, which would create a regulatory framework for cryptocurrencies, had stalled amid concerns among Democrats and some Republicans that it had insufficient ethics and illicit finance safeguards and could destabilize the banking system by creating more competition for deposits.
This morning, GOP senators Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, John Boozman of Arkansas and Tim Scott of South Carolina said the new text incorporated “126 substantive changes made at the request of Democrats”.
But it’s still unclear if it has enough support to reach the 60-vote threshold needed to pass a key procedural vote tomorrow that could determine the bill’s fate, while the banking industry remained opposed to the text, an industry official told Reuters.
“After a year of intense daily bipartisan negotiations, this bill is ready,” Lummis said in a statement. “Democrats got what they wanted; now they need to take yes for an answer.”
Democrats have been pushing, in particular, for the text to include stricter restrictions on public officeholders profiting off their own crypto ventures, an effort in part aimed at Donald Trump’s World Liberty Financial. Trump in June disclosed that he had made $1.4bn off his crypto ventures.
The new text includes rules put forth by senators Thom Tillis, a Republican, and Democrat Ruben Gallego. It includes giving state attorneys general more power to enforce the restrictions.
“President Trump voluntarily agreed to unprecedented ethics restrictions, holding every federally elected official, judge, and their spouses to some of the toughest ethics restrictions in US history,” Lummis said in the statement.
Spokespeople for Gallego and Tillis did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment on whether they endorsed the new text.
The new draft also includes new protections for bank deposits, and protects consumers with new guardrails on affiliate trading, clarifies the applicability of state consumer protection laws and protects software developers, the Republican senators said.
However, the banking industry continues to have concerns about language that would allow crypto players to offer rewards on dollar-backed tokens known as stablecoins, the industry official told Reuters.
A number of local governments are also filing a similar lawsuit, challenging the new DHS rule set to take effect.
Zohran Mamdani, the New York mayor, is one of the officials leading the charge.
“The new public charge rule not only sweeps aside more than a century of established law, it is intentionally vague as a means of creating uncertainty and fear to isolate immigrant New Yorkers,” he said at a press conference on Monday.
He added:
This is an undisguised effort to strip New Yorkers of the services they rely on, the public benefits they are entitled to. Families, including those with children who are US citizens, have already begun to forego essential services like SNAP, Medicaid, and affordable housing out of the fear that if they use these programs, immigration officers could use it as justification to deny them a future in our country.
Two dozen states sue Trump administration over rule to make it harder to get green cards
Two dozen states and the District of Columbia have sued the Trump administration over a rule that would make it harder for adults to get a green card.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy, due to take effect on Friday, grants immigration officials greater authority to reject green cards if applicants are deemed likely to rely on public assistance programs like food stamps and Medicaid.
Federal law already requires those seeking to become US permanent residents to prove they will not be a burden to the US – also known as a “public charge” – but the new rule includes broader range of programs that could disqualify them. The measure essentially rescinds a Biden-era rule which excluded non-cash benefits from consideration when adjudicating a green card application, and revives a policy from Trump’s first term in office.
“This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, healthcare coverage and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled,” Letitia James, the New York attorney general, said in a statement.
The states argue that the new rule exceeds the longstanding interpretation of the public charge provision passed by Congress.
In response to another federal judge blocking the Trump’s order that directs the US Postal Service to tighten mail-in voting requirements, the NAACP has welcomed the injunction after they sued the administration.
“The election is just 49 days away. We urge the supreme court to reject this administration’s request to green light this unlawful scheme and leave in place our mailing voting system which is safe, secure and orderly. We will always stand up for voters and continue to fight this administration’s voter suppression attempts,” said Kristen Clarke, NAACP’s general counsel.
Top Senate Democrat calls for all-chamber meeting with Trump administration about AI guardrails
Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader has called for an all-senators briefing with key administration officials to discuss the administration’s actions to regulate “responsible” development of artificial intelligence, and “stopping China’s advancement of AI”.
“I have long argued that we must keep the US as the global leader in AI innovation and security,” Schumer, a Democratic senator from New York said in a statement. “But that innovation must be coupled with serious guardrails that earn the trust of the American public.”
Schumer pointed to the “warning bells” over the weekend from leading AI company CEOs who called for the slow down of technology development, and the reports from Anthropic whistleblowers last week, who said their employers were acting irresponsibly by “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”.
The top Democrat said that if companies “won’t hold themselves accountable, we will. And if Trump does not act, Congress must”.
Today, as Congress returns from recess, a key House panel is set to consider a bill which would punish Russia and countries that buy its petroleum exports over the invasion of Ukraine.
The bill would impose new sanctions and visa bans on Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and top military commanders, as well as put tariffs of up to 500% on the country’s exports. And it would also allow Trumpto impose levies of up to 100% on goods from countries that are the top five importers of Russian oil and gas.
While supportive of the mission, many Democrats fear that the legislation would give the president latitude to implement more tariffs. The Senate passed a version of the bill last month, but the House rules committee will vote on it today before it can head to the floor for a full vote.
'I don't think Americans should be scared of anything': Vance tries to quell concerns about AI regulation
Ahead of traveling to Kansas City, Missouri, vice-president JD Vance told reporters that he doesn’t think Americans “should be scared of anything” when it comes to concerns about AI regulation.
The vice-president attempted to quell concerns after leading AI companies said they would welcome moderating advancement.
“I think what the president has said is we want to be smart about making sure we stay on top of the risks. I don’t think Americans should be scared of anything … There are downsides to anything, and that’s certainly true of AI,” Vance said on the tarmac.
He added that the best way to implement guardrails would be a “consensus between both Congress and the administration”.
Vance also noted that he was skeptical of AI companies “begging” the government for increased regulation. “It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan Horse. So I think we just have to be careful about this,” he said.

articles.title: ‘They just want the war to end’: Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina on why she believes most Russians are pacifists — and whether the opposition can reach them
articles.body:
‘They just want the war to end’: Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina on why she believes most Russians are pacifists — and whether the opposition can reach them
After the Yabloko party — which ran on antiwar slogans and briefly gave hope to many Russians — was barred from the State Duma election, the opposition, both inside Russia and in emigration, has been debating what voting strategies to adopt now. The Bereg cooperative spoke with Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina about the hopes tied to Yabloko, what the election results might actually change, the divide between those who left and those who stayed, and the prospects for a new democracy. Meduza is publishing the interview in full.
— Did you expect the authorities to let Yabloko run its campaign and compete for votes, or did you assume they would block it?
— There was a sense that the Kremlin had its own separate line, or at least an internal debate, about softening the regime. The wavering was obvious: Yabloko was registered and approved, after all. Perhaps [some officials] pinned their hopes on the negotiations that began after Trump took office, hoping for reconciliation. But it’s become clear recently that things are actually headed toward continuing the war, toward finishing it off — and the negotiations have been shelved indefinitely.
The period when negotiations were actually underway was, of course, full of hope, and traces of that hope still lingered this past spring. Yabloko being allowed to run would have signaled that the negotiating track was still being considered — and had they been barred, that would have signaled the opposite.
— Did you notice growing interest in Yabloko?
— Activists really did start talking about voting for Yabloko. There was enthusiasm among a certain segment of society — people who had been to at least one protest in their lives.
— What was the mood among these people after the party’s list was disqualified?
— They hoped for a miracle. It didn’t happen, but life goes on — there’s no sense that life has stopped. Young people who came to politics for the first time probably feel the disappointment more deeply. Those who are older have already lived through so many political disappointments…
— You’ve surely heard the opposition debate various election strategies: boycotting, voting for anyone but United Russia, or backing a specific party like New People or Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF). But this debate mostly plays out outside Russia, among opposition figures abroad. Does it exist inside the country?
— The mood is roughly this: “How much longer can this go on? Nothing depends on this, nothing will change because of it.” Among a certain segment of true Yabloko supporters, there’s talk of spoiling the ballot or not showing up at all.
Protest voting can produce political consequences, but they’re so illusory, let’s say, that it doesn’t feel worth the energy overall. The idea of voting for any party at all, which used to excite people, doesn’t excite me anymore.
— What are these illusory consequences?
— There’s a pragmatic logic to voting for one of the parliamentary parties, but that logic only applies in a crisis scenario. During turbulence, when the system becomes unbalanced, change always happens through institutionalized players, actors within the system. If several establishment parties won a slightly higher share of the vote, that would, in theory, position them to become those players.
The vote share [for them] would have to be large enough that it couldn’t be masked by fraud — and right now, it’s far from certain that’s even possible. With electronic voting, there may be no limit to fraud at all.
There’s also symbolic voting, which doesn’t inspire me at all — going to a polling station and writing in Yabloko on the ballot. That’s unlikely to accomplish anything, and as for a clean conscience… Honestly, I’ve cleansed mine so many times already that I don’t really need to. Especially since it’s not even a unified strategy — “Smart Voting” has shown that, for the most part, it doesn’t produce results.
You’re choosing one cannibal over another. Let everyone decide for themselves — the main message is just: go vote, and decide [who to vote for] on your own, however you want.
— So voters can still show the authorities their discontent?
— I think the government knows all about that discontent. It just no longer takes society into account — its mood is well known. Instead, it works on society through violence, aggression, and a steady drip of one nasty thing after another. They do something nasty, wait a while, make some noise, let people get used to it, then take the next small step. Society manages to adapt, to adjust. People have even somehow adapted to the shortage of gasoline.
— And you?
— We fill up at night and only drive when it’s absolutely necessary. There’s even something environmentally friendly about it — you ride a scooter or walk to the nearest store. Everyone now keeps a gas canister in the trunk, like in the 1990s. And we just keep living.
— Perhaps people started supporting Yabloko precisely because they’re tired of constantly adapting?
— People started supporting Yabloko for another important reason too. I wrote an article called “5 Discourses Around the War,” where I showed how the antiwar and pro-war discourses diverged.
But the largest and most important layer of opinion was never expressed publicly anywhere. Most people were pro-Putin and antiwar. They had no public spokespeople at all, but they could be called pacifists. [In the media space, it’s assumed that] you’re either pro-Putin and pro-war, or anti-Putin and antiwar. There’s also a variant — anti-Putin but pro-war — which exists among Z bloggers.
People who were pro-Putin and antiwar had no talking heads of their own — until Viktoria Bonya. They were a silent majority. When negotiations with Trump began, and there was hope for a ceasefire, they thought: “Fine, we’ll wait — they’ve started negotiating, so it will probably be alright.”
A year passed, the negotiations went nowhere, problems kept mounting, and that silent majority’s voice began to emerge — we saw it in Bonya’s statement and others like it. The authorities tried to silence those voices, and in response, this group’s views began shifting toward an anti-Putin position.
The antiwar discourse split long ago into a pro-Ukrainian strand and a pacifist strand. Lev Shlosberg represents the latter, and so do I. Most people in Russia identify with the pacifist discourse — most citizens were raised as pacifists in the Soviet Union. Everyone sang Let There Always Be Sunshine, and today’s young people sang it in school too.
Not everyone within that broad pacifist discourse is ready to come out against Putin. Some of them supported Yabloko and started moving toward an anti-Putin position. The party doesn’t directly say it’s against Putin — it focuses instead on its opposition to the war.
And that’s a smart approach — it draws in more and more of these people, because they’re for peace but not yet ready to talk about Putin. The next step for them is lifting the taboo on criticizing Putin, the way the taboo on discussing the war was lifted.
— So, to win over public sympathy, you shouldn’t talk about Putin, because it’s still too soon?
— People react to events in bursts. For example, when the gasoline problems began, open rejection of the Russian authorities appeared, in some cases even hatred. But it’s not directed at Putin personally — he’s too sacred a figure. It’s impersonal hatred toward “the bosses” in general.
The position favoring a Ukrainian victory resonates with hardly anyone in Russia. These people exist, but there aren’t many of them. The old opposition can speak loudly because it’s in emigration. But, in my view, this position will never be shared by the majority in Russia.
— And what position could it share? Accepting an outcome, where neither Ukraine nor Russia wins?
— That’s the most likely outcome. But the trend [in Russia] has changed: previously, holding the position “let’s have peace, and it doesn’t matter who wins” wasn’t punished as a matter of principle — now, it seems to me, it’s starting to be. The Shlosberg case showed that, as did [Andrei] Klepach’s dismissal. You can no longer question the idea of victory.
— Does the silent majority need this victory?
— They just want the war to end. It seems the victory narrative isn’t aimed at ordinary citizens but at the most active, pro-war segment of society — maybe at Putin himself too, who probably belongs to that segment as well.
There’s a segment of society that isn’t ready to let this go without a victory — they’ve paid too high a price over these four years: many of their people have died, a great deal has been invested.
But that’s a small share. Most people don’t care, as long as it all ends. And what kind of victory would that even be? What is victory, really? People generally aren’t very interested — they’re ready to accept whatever they’re offered as victory.
— Maxim Katz believes the opposition in emigration is largely to blame for Yabloko being barred — that they showed support at the wrong time. Do you share that view?
— I think it sped up the process, but Yabloko would have been barred anyway — maybe a bit later, and the campaign would have run a little longer. I don’t know whether they would have expanded it [nationwide] or not. In Veliky Novgorod, banners reading “For Peace!” and “For Yabloko!” are still hanging, because they’re running for the regional assembly there and have an active local cell. In Moscow, there was nothing visible at all — zero.
The problem is that no one negotiates with anyone, no one talks things through — just like Putin doesn’t with Volodymyr Zelensky. Yabloko never coordinated with the opposition [in emigration] on whether support was needed, or what kind. And the opposition never approached Yabloko in advance to discuss the form or timing of support.
I never publicly support anyone unless asked to, because I know my support could do harm — even though I’m only designated as a “foreign agent” by Russian authorities, and I live in Russia. When you have “undesirable” status, or something worse, you have to handle this very carefully. It seems to me that some kind of ethic around this should have developed by now, over these years. But it hasn’t, unfortunately — everyone tries to distance themselves from everyone else.
— Maybe the Kremlin is making an effort to set opposition figures against each other?
— The Kremlin didn’t need to make any effort, because Yabloko never really entered into negotiations with anyone — or did so only rarely. I can’t complain here, since I’ve collaborated with Yabloko a great deal and I’m very grateful to them for that. But I know plenty of stories where they simply wouldn’t negotiate with the rest of the opposition. And the rest of the opposition didn’t come to them either.
There’s also an additional factor now: media visibility. The laws of the mass-media market demand an immediate public reaction to the political agenda, and that factor plays a bigger role than the political one.
For many well-known opposition figures in emigration, the public sphere just comes down to mass media — an old model built around a single source of information. There can be competition among several major players, but it’s neither networked nor horizontal. You can only take part in that process as a unit within the mass — through your like.
The public environment needs to be built differently, starting today. Social networks, when they first emerged, offered hope that it could be. But in the end, opposition actors continued to mirror the existing order — the power-based model for organizing the public sphere [and don’t create platforms for discussion, only broadcast their own views].
— In your view, what election strategy is the Kremlin pursuing?
— The authorities used to feel a need to simulate elections more convincingly. In our district, there was genuine competition in the 2021 elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, and strong competition across Moscow generally.
Now the authorities aren’t allowing anything genuine at all. They’re suppressing turnout — it’s very important to them that only their own people show up at the polls. In Moscow, only single-mandate candidates are running any kind of campaign; in our district, an SVO veteran has been at it for months already.
There’s also electronic voting. In my view, the entire electronic vote in the last Moscow City Duma elections was fabricated. I went to my polling station on Sunday at 7 p.m. and voted with a paper ballot — mine was the first one in the ballot box. People did come to the polling station, but everyone there was made to vote electronically.
— Observers say electronic voting can’t be monitored at all.
— There will still be plenty of paper voting in the regions. But the observer movement has grown quite weak — few people volunteer as observers anymore, and all the active organizations have been crushed. It probably takes society some time to understand that no public leaders or organizations are going to appear anymore, and that people need to organize on their own here.
There’s a big open question: are there limits to fraud under current conditions? Observer theory holds that every instance of fraud has its limits — that you can’t falsify more than a certain percentage. But does that rule still hold now?
— If the limits on fraud are loose enough to manufacture any result for United Russia, even an implausible one, and the authorities use that leeway — what reaction would that provoke in society?
— In my view, it’s the youngest part of society — the ones who suddenly believed in something — who could end up demoralized and disillusioned. On the whole, people don’t place much hope in elections and are unlikely to be disappointed. In advanced political thought, which runs a bit ahead of political reality, elections as a symbol of democracy have long been discredited.
The discrediting of elections will help give rise to new forms of democracy in this country. They’re already emerging, and this alternative experience could become the basis for a new political philosophy, practice, and democracy here. But these are lengthy processes.
— Are you talking about horizontal interaction between people?
— Yes, these are horizontal forms. Some communities, for instance, have devised complex combinations of lottery and voting for decision-making. People in small communities choose leaders simply because they know them, and leaders rotate quickly. That includes political communities, women’s communities, and local interest clubs.
I know a theater group that stages its own plays with its own money and tours with them. This amateur theater has its own forms of democracy, its own forms of decision-making. A director originally brought the group together and made the decisions, but after he died, the group decided not to disband and to run things themselves instead. Now they look for directors and make democratic decisions about whom to hire.
Horizontal structures exist all over the country — gardening co-ops, homeowners’ associations. The whole country is threaded through with a variety of democratic formats.
— Do the authorities notice them? The Kremlin is now promoting the concept of “social architecture” — supposedly not a political technology, but engagement with citizens and communities on social projects.
— They have this new term because they consider only geopolitics to be politics. Of course, they’re not going to build real democracy or real democratic institutions — they always build an imitation.
But hijacking the agenda [from the state] was dangerous in the 2010s. Now the top leadership cares about only one thing — the ”special military operation” — and has no time for such games.
I think it’s dangerous that the very people who want to build a different Russia — not a Limonov-style one, but a genuinely different one — don’t fully grasp the importance of real democratic alternatives. They’re still playing by the old rules. Under the old system, you can outplay those in power, break the regime, build another one, but fundamentally it will still rest on all the same original patterns.
In my view, we need to come up with new ideas, find them within society, help them develop — and then a new political event will happen. We need to dream, to build utopias — that’s very important. We’re going through a phase of major historical shift right now. We all sense it. People have been talking about it for 100 years already.
When I was studying cultural studies in the late 1990s and early 2000s, everyone talked about this major shift. I really hoped the changes would come without violence. But, unfortunately, we entered this historical cycle along with it.
— You’re speaking in terms of a broad historical framework. What if we narrow it down to talk about the so-called ones who left and the ones who stayed? People can presumably be divided based on whether they emigrated, but can these groups be generalized by their views and convictions? Is there some essential conflict between them?
— I don’t think there’s any conflict between “those who left” and “those who stayed” — people communicate with each other. But there is a conflict between public discourses. When that gets translated into personal terms — explaining someone’s views and positions by whether they left or stayed, as if that determines who they are, [that’s wrong]…
Your everyday reality probably still shapes your perception. Perhaps a larger share of nonconformists — people willing to break many ties — ended up among those who left. These people often have a hard time accepting others, other ways of life. But claiming that nonconformists left and conformists stayed is an oversimplification. Often, leaving or staying was simply a forced decision.
— On July 2, you published a post on Facebook calling for an end to the cycle of “retaliatory strikes” between Russia and Ukraine. At the time, some politicians and activists criticized you for “abstract pacifism” and “equalizing morality” — or, more gently, for an unfortunate choice of words. How did you feel about those accusations then, and how do you feel about them now?
— It was unpleasant that people resorted to personal attacks instead of debating the ideas.
Naturally, I never intended to equate the aggressor with the victim — I don’t even understand what’s meant by that [in the critical posts]. I was talking about children. They’re not aggressors. Children are always victims.
Not long ago, I talked with some random people about this — about the drones. People were complaining, and I asked them: “You understand why this is happening, who started all of it, right?” They answered: “The main thing is for it all to end soon, for them to somehow reach an agreement. It doesn’t matter how, let them just agree.”
People aren’t demanding “payback” — they’re reacting like pacifists, not militarists bent on revenge. Hatred toward Ukrainians in Russia hasn’t spread as much as I feared back in July, after all. What people have developed instead is hatred toward the war and those who continue it.
— How do you think Russians will discuss these painful topics a year, five years, 10 years after the war ends? Or is this not really a matter of time, but of something else?
— If it all ends within a year — and there is hope for that — people will want to forget all of it. This is a painful experience, a major trauma for society.
Over a 5–10 year horizon, everything will depend on how events unfold. If Russia changes, I think the question of responsibility will come up eventually. But in my view, those changes will be gradual rather than revolutionary. After some time, people will start asking themselves what they did wrong, how they let this happen. I, at least, hope for that.
Right now people are in a state of trauma, and it’s pointless to ask them these questions, especially since ordinary citizens didn’t make the actual decisions. So right now, it seems to me, these conversations just pour fuel on the fire of the war.
Dialogue is possible in principle, even between the most radical people. Except… you know, it’s already a bit of a broken record: “Well, you over there.” — “Well, you should repent.” — “Well, you won’t understand us.” You open Facebook, read all this, and close it again.
We can all understand each other, especially when we want to. Jürgen Habermas called this communicative ethics. A genuine communicative action is an effort to understand another person, not to convince them otherwise, humiliate them, or prove them wrong. Even people who don’t share a common language share common facial expressions — you can smile, and that smile will be understood in every language, by every people.
Communities that work toward understanding others, toward building discussions and debates, are really valuable, and there are plenty of them in Russia right now. Don’t take this as me criticizing “those who left” again — no, I mean public figures in emigration, as political actors.
Unfortunately, many of them are once again resorting to old methods: “Let’s not try to understand the other person — let’s just explain to them that they’re a fool, let’s shut them up.” In doing so, they’re only perpetuating those same old habits: the absence of dialogue, the drive toward total unanimity.
— When the war ends, will Russia change?
— The end of the war will bring relief. It could also become a trigger for change — some kind of democratization movement might begin, which would ultimately turn the wheel. Either that turn will come from above, or it will be some joint movement, from above and below. History is unpredictable. But I’d like the change not to happen too quickly.
If it’s the proverbial short-term “window of opportunity,” it will lead to unfounded changes imposed from above. Someone will appear who says, once again: “We’ll solve everything in 500 days.”
People can’t handle that, which is why I think the pace of change matters. It’s important that changes be rooted, that their direction be shaped with society’s participation. Society needs to be brought into a conversation about its own future — and that can and should start now. Otherwise, we’ll end up again in a situation where one part of society wins and another loses, and on the next turn, revanchism sets in: the losing side will want to replay everything all over again.

articles.title: German intelligence report warns of rising Chinese, Russian spy threat
articles.body:
German intelligence report warns of rising Chinese, Russian spy threat
A report by Germany’s counter-intelligence agency said some surveillance activities targeting military infrastructure can be linked to China
Germany’s military counter-intelligence agency, known as MAD, has warned of a growing threat from hybrid attacks and the use of recruited contract agents, or low-level agents, saying Germany is a “prioritised target of Russian espionage activities”.
According to the agency’s annual report released on Monday, it cited Germany’s geostrategic position in Europe and Nato the expansion of the Bundeswehr and the introduction of new weapons systems as reasons for the heightened targeting.
“The hybrid threat situation in Germany has continued to deteriorate,” MAD says. These include cyberattacks, drone attacks, attempts at political influence, and disruptive attacks targeting transport, energy facilities and telecommunications.
MAD said the potential threat of sabotage by low-level agents has also increased significantly. The report does not provide comparative figures, which could lead adversaries to draw conclusions from the data.

articles.title: Ex-CIA boss was steps away when Russian drone hit Ukrainian train
articles.body:
- Retired Gen. David Petraeus said a jet-powered Geran drone, not the standard Geran-2, struck a train engine near Ukraine's border with Poland on September 13.
- Petraeus was at Yahodyn station when the strike occurred, minutes after a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson had departed for Poland.
Retired Gen. David Petraeus said the Russian drone that struck a train near Ukraine’s border with Poland on September 13 was a jet-powered version of Russia’s Geran/Shahed attack drone, adding a detail Ukrainian officials had not specified in their own statements on the strike.
Petraeus, a former CIA director and retired four-star U.S. Army general, was aboard a separate train at Yahodyn station, about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border, when the drone hit the locomotive of a nearby Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train early Sunday. Ukraine’s state rail operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, confirmed his presence at the station and said there were no reports of casualties. A diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt and security advisers from several European Union states had left the same station minutes earlier and had already crossed into Poland by the time of the strike.
“A Geran jet-powered drone hit the engine of the train on the track,” Petraeus wrote in a comment to The Defence Blog’s editor-in-chief on LinkedIn. He added that his own train had already passed through Ukrainian customs and was next to the one that was hit, close to the Polish border.
Ukrainian officials had said only that the strike involved a drone and that it was “quite likely” the diplomatic train, not the stationary locomotive, was the intended target. Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces were targeting rail infrastructure in western Ukraine used to move military supplies, without addressing the specific drone type. Petraeus’s account is the first to specify that the drone involved was a jet-powered Geran variant rather than the piston-engine Geran-2, also known as the Shahed-136, that makes up the bulk of Russia’s long-range drone fleet.
Ukraine’s Air Force had said the broader overnight barrage that day, in which Russia launched 863 drones nationwide, included a newer jet-powered drone alongside standard Geran-2s, Gerbera decoys and S8000 Banderol missile-carrying drones. Jet propulsion gives a drone higher speed than the piston-engine Geran-2, making it harder for air defenses to intercept.
Petraeus has traveled to Ukraine repeatedly since Russia’s 2022 invasion in an advisory capacity. He now serves as a partner at the investment firm KKR and chairs its Global Institute. Neither Ukrainian officials nor Russia’s Defense Ministry has confirmed the specific drone type Petraeus described.
The strike came as poor weather grounded much of western Ukraine in low cloud that day and coincided with the departure of multiple foreign delegations from Kyiv following a security conference there. Analysts, including French open-source researcher Clément Molin, have said the cloud cover made it harder for Ukrainian air-defense crews to visually track incoming drones.

articles.title: What Trump Doesn’t Understand About Xi
articles.body:
What Trump Doesn’t Understand About Xi
The Chinese leader cares very little about personal rapport.
President Trump will host Xi Jinping for a state visit on September 24, once again putting his claimed bonhomie with the Chinese leader at the center of the relations between the two superpowers. But Trump’s insistence on the importance of this personal rapport shows just how little he understands his adversary.
I have been studying Xi ever since he became China’s heir apparent, and I became an analyst at the CIA in the waning days of the George W. Bush administration. I spent years deciphering Xi for U.S. presidents as the intelligence community’s top expert on Xi. And I spent two years as the director for China at the National Security Council, where I staffed all of President Biden’s interactions with Xi and coordinated diplomacy with China across the U.S. government.
For a decade now, Trump has oscillated between courting and skirmishing with Xi. After his first term, Trump called Xi a friend and described him as someone he knew well. His experience with Xi seems to have led him to believe that he has unique, firsthand insights into China’s leader that his staff and advisers lack; in the past year, he has excluded even his close confidants, such as Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, from intensive diplomacy with China, and has acted practically as his own China desk officer.
Trump’s go-to stratagem for gaining leverage with Xi has been to be unpredictable, or at least to try to be. Yet in Trump’s second term, Xi has surprised Trump more often than Trump has surprised him. That is because Xi’s modus operandi, at home and abroad, is that of a jack-in-the-box: He winds up patiently over years, sometimes decades, and then pops at the propitious moment. The result is always startling.
Xi rose to become China’s leader in large part by presenting himself as having the steady hands needed to restart stalled economic reforms without upsetting the comfortable gentlemen’s agreements that kept the Communist Party’s factional rivalries in check. But once Xi secured power, he launched a blistering campaign against the very party elites who had pulled him up.
Xi’s steeliness has caught Trump off guard, just as it did his Chinese colleagues. At the time of Trump’s first term, Xi was accustomed to playing politics as a quiet, intense poker match, in which the Chinese leader read the opposing players and considered his own cards with characteristic subtlety. Trump, meanwhile, approached politics and policy making more like a gambler on a hot streak at one of the casinos he owned. During his first encounter with Trump, at Mar-a-Lago in 2017, Xi learned about U.S. air strikes on Syria over a beautiful piece of chocolate cake. He spent the years in between Trump’s first and second terms winding up to deal with a president whose M.O. he now understood—and preparing to pop up when the moment was right.
That moment came early in Trump’s second term. In April 2025, the U.S. president rolled out his “Liberation Day” tariffs, which included some that amounted to a de facto embargo on China. Xi surprised Trump by being the only world leader to retaliate rather than conciliate. Trump was ultimately forced to fold.
In the run-up to the two leaders’ summit in Seoul last fall, Xi again surprised Trump’s team—this time by unfurling an expansive set of export controls on rare earth elements, which ultimately prompted the U.S. to roll back its own export controls on China. Beijing’s willingness to escalate was a remarkable departure from a previous pattern of downplaying differences ahead of such summits, and it underscored that Xi was more interested in curtailing Washington’s ability to target China than in striking a deal.
Accordingly, the meeting in Seoul, and Trump’s subsequent visit to Beijing in May, produced little beyond relatively minor commercial agreements affecting specific firms and sectors. The Trump administration, undoubtedly disappointed by the lack of any meaningful deal to emerge from these summits, chose to emphasize Trump’s efforts to deepen his rapport with Xi. The president evidently believes this personal relationship will allow him to secure deals that advance American interests.
This expectation has no observable foundation in Xi’s 14-year rule. Even by the standards of authoritarian rulers, such as Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Xi has shown himself to be unsentimental about personal relationships—including those with members of his own inner circle, to say nothing of the leader of China’s principal geopolitical rival. Xi is very different from Putin in this regard. Whereas Putin takes extravagant risks on the international stage but is loath to hold his associates accountable for incompetence, Xi is just the opposite. He is calculating and measured in international politics but pitiless in jettisoning even longtime associates for perceived malfeasance.
In January, Xi dismissed his military’s top officer, General Zhang Youxia. The relationship between Xi and Zhang went back decades, extending not just to their childhoods but all the way back to their fathers, who were comrades in arms in China’s ferocious civil war. Four years ago, Xi deferred Zhang’s retirement, keeping him on board to help manage the world’s largest and second-most-capable military. We do not know what motivated Xi to oust Zhang, but given the history between the two men, the act was as brutal and unexpected as anything in a season finale of Game of Thrones.
Xi’s approach to Washington has been similarly dispassionate. During Trump’s visit to Beijing, the American president lavished praise on Xi, only for the Chinese leader to respond with stoic indifference.
Trump’s desire to parlay personal charisma into deals may be one of his least idiosyncratic qualities. In fact, there is something about the impulse that is quintessentially American. Even—perhaps especially—for a Beltway outsider, ascending the American political ladder requires a tremendous amount of glad-handing and personal magnetism, if not charm. Those who reach its pinnacle often assume that the same qualities will serve them on the international stage. Joe Biden rose through the Senate, which required cordiality and the ability to strike deals with rivals. George W. Bush and Bill Clinton were known for their affability. Overbearing friendliness might even be described as our national affect.
By contrast, Xi grew up in a system that punished openness and personal dynamism. His father’s boss and mentor, the reformer Hu Yaobang, whose death in 1989 sparked the protests in Tiananmen Square, was known for his outspokenness, which played a crucial role in his political demise. Hu’s ouster extinguished freewheeling politicking from the ranks of China’s leadership ever after.
Going into his next encounter with Xi, Trump seems to genuinely believe that he has the upper hand. Yet an unsettling split screen has accompanied every summit of his second term. In Seoul, Xi walked into the meeting having just outlined the five-year plan for China’s development through 2030. By contrast, Trump was in the midst of the longest government shutdown in U.S. history. In May, Xi hosted Trump for a meeting that Trump had earlier postponed because of the war in Iran, which was going badly. Xi now plans to follow his state visit to Washington with a major party meeting to lay the groundwork for his fourth five-year term, which will start next year. Trump, meanwhile, will be at best a lame-duck president within weeks of the summit—or worse, if the Democrats are able to take back the House or the Senate.
The contrast evident at these meetings with Trump has surely reinforced Xi’s view of the United States as a declining but dangerous power, and of China as an ascendant one. Xi believes that time is on his side, so he does not need a deal. He’s happy to perpetuate an uneasy stalemate through a pantomime of rapport with Trump. In the meantime, Xi is winding up for the fifth U.S presidential administration of his tenure, whatever it may bring.
All statements of fact, opinion, or analysis expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the official positions or views of the U.S. government. Nothing in the contents should be construed as asserting or implying U.S.-government authentication of information or endorsement of the author's views.

articles.title: Ukraine Must Attack Russia’s Missile Plants to Win War, MITS Capital CEO Says
articles.body:
Ukraine cannot defend its way to victory over Russia, shooting down missiles one-at-a-time, it must attack the sources, according to Perry Boyle, co-founder and CEO of MITS Capital, one of Ukraine’s largest defense-industry investment groups.
Speaking at the Yalta European Strategy (YES) forum, held by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation in Kyiv on Sept. 11-12, Boyle said the world does not have enough air defense systems to fully protect Ukraine, and a strategy built solely around intercepting Russian missiles and drones is doomed to fail.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
MITS Capital, based in Kyiv and New York, was co-founded by Boyle – a retired veteran of US investment banking who worked at firms including Thomas Weisel Partners and SAC Capital – with Ukrainian volunteer Denys Gurak in 2022, Boyle told Kyiv Post in an interview in September 2025.
Interfax-Ukraine quoted Boyle:
“The only strategy that will work here is to convince your partners that they need to defeat Russia, and for Ukraine to attack Russia’s economy and the Russian factories that produce missiles. Once the missiles are launched from Russia, you have no defense, and today you are not using your long-range attack potential to the full – I guarantee you that.”
Boyle also argued that Kyiv’s push to attract foreign capital into its defense-industrial complex has been undermined by its own policy. He said:
Putin’s Economic Growth Claims Diverge From IMF Data
“There has been very little foreign investment in Ukraine’s defense industry, partly because of Ukraine’s policy of favoring foreign companies operating on its territory over domestic ones. Your partners are trying to get your technology as cheaply as possible while investing in Ukraine as little as possible.”
Under current conditions, he added, it would make far more business sense for MITS Capital to operate out of Poland or Czechia than Ukraine – though he said the government and the Verkhovna Rada could still act to change the policy. Boyle said:
“Ultimately, if you can’t change your partners’ narrative that Russia must be defeated in Ukraine, there will be no deal with Russia on peace – we know that, and Ukraine will become the next Georgia. That’s the core of the problem.”
As of September 2025, MITS had invested in 11 companies, including ground-drone maker Tencore and frontline communications firm Teletactica, Kyiv Post has reported.
That same month, the fund launched MITS Industries, a Denmark-based holding company uniting Ukrainian manufacturers such as signals-intelligence firm Infozahyst and electronic-warfare producer Unwave.
At YES 2026, Boyle described MITS’s portfolio as having grown to several dozen companies supplying Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
Among the most recent investments, MITS Capital invested in Dropla Tech, a Danish-Ukrainian defense technology company whose AI system has confirmed more than 5,000 explosive-threat detections in Ukraine.
