articles.title: North Korea says held 'joint firepower attack drill' of long-range artillery, missile units
articles.body:
Faisal Mahmud
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
North Korea said on Monday that its military conducted a "joint firepower attack drill" involving long-range artillery and missile units, a day after the US, South Korea and Japan concluded joint military exercises, state news agency KCNA reported.
The drill was held on Saturday and involved selected subunits from five artillery and missile units of the Korean People's Army (KPA).
The exercise involved "new combat systems," including various attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, large-caliber thermobaric multiple rocket launchers and tactical ballistic missiles.
KPA Marshal Pak Jong Chon, vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party, and Artillery Bureau Director Maj Gen Yu Chang Son supervised the exercise.
KCNA claimed all strike systems hit their targets with "100 percent hit accuracy," demonstrating their ability to conduct simultaneous concentrated attacks.
Yu said such exercises were intended to strengthen the military's strategic counterattack posture and improve the rapid-response capabilities of units during emergencies.
The US military said on Friday it was tracking multiple North Korean missile launches but assessed they posed no immediate threat to US personnel, territory or regional allies.
The launches came a day after South Korea, the US and Japan concluded their five-day trilateral Freedom Edge naval exercise in international waters off South Korea's southern Jeju Island.

articles.title: BREAKING: Trump claims Ukraine, Russia agree to halt strikes on energy targets
articles.body:
BREAKING: Trump claims Ukraine, Russia agree to halt strikes on energy targets, Kyiv unaware of deal
U.S. President Donald Trump claimed on Sept. 14 that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to halt strikes on "energy targets," as fuel prices continue to rise worldwide.
"Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy Targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" Trump said in a Truth Social post.
"The World's Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine war, not Iran."
Neither Ukraine nor Russia has confirmed that such a deal had been struck. Roughly an hour after Trump's post, Zelensky responded, saying he was "not sure" of Russia's desire to adhere to any such agreement.
"If the partners are ready to ensure Russia’s real desire not to strike our electricity, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food movement, then we are, of course, ready to ensure the corresponding absence of our strikes," Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
"The war must be ended. And a de-escalation step regarding critical infrastructure could be the first step towards peace. We are waiting for details from our partners."
A top Ukrainian energy official, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, said they had not heard of any such energy ceasefire.
The announcement comes just a day after Trump directly blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for rising diesel prices — including in the U.S., where the price soared to a record $6.23 per gallon ($1.65 per liter) over the weekend.
"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump said on Sept 13. "Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he's causing a shortage of diesel."
"We spoke to Mr. Zelensky about it... This isn't done by the Middle East."
Trump's war against Iran has knocked out more than 20% of Middle Eastern refining capacity and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, which previously carried roughly a fifth of global oil supplies.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has continued targeting Russian oil infrastructure as part of its broader effort to disrupt fuel supplies and reduce revenues that Moscow uses to finance its war against Ukraine.
The strike campaign, which has escalated significantly in scale and scope over the last 12 months thanks to the advancements in Ukraine's arsenal of long-range drones, has been a crucial lever of offensive pressure for Kyiv.
The announcement is not the first time that a limited "energy truce" has been proposed in Russia's war against Ukraine.
The idea that both sides cease such attacks was raised numerous times during the fruitless peace talks mediated by the Trump administration over summer 2025.
On Sept. 13, Zelensky announced plans to discuss halting Russian and Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea during a possible meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump next week in New York.
The meeting could take place on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly between Sept. 21-23 if the presidents' schedules align. The talks would come as U.S.-led efforts to broker a broader peace deal remain stalled over Russia's territorial demands.
"We are open to a maritime ceasefire, as well as an energy ceasefire. I plan to discuss all of this," Zelensky said in an interview with Ukraine's national television aired on Sept. 13.
Russia's reaction to Kyiv's recent proposals has been muted so far.
On Sept. 10 Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Kyiv is not offering a "permanent settlement that would fully align with (Russian) interests" and merely seeks a truce in an area that is Ukraine's "Achilles' heel."

articles.title: Iran tried to intimidate Saudi Arabia - it may have made Riyadh more powerful instead - opinion
articles.body:
Tehran can drive up oil prices. What it cannot control is the rising price of Saudi cooperation.
Iran wants Saudi Arabia to remember a simple geography fact: it may be rich, heavily armed, and close to Washington, but it still sits on the Gulf and is dependent on energy routes Tehran can threaten.
The current war is exposing the flaw in that strategy.
Iran can make the Strait of Hormuz more dangerous, push oil prices higher, and pressure US President Donald Trump through American gas prices.
But Tehran’s own ability to profit from those higher prices has been crippled, while Saudi Arabia enters the crisis with infrastructure that allows it to bypass Hormuz and a regional position that is becoming more valuable by the day.
In other words, the more Iran raises the cost of confrontation, the more it may also raise the price of Riyadh.
And that is where the story gets bigger than oil.
Washington needs Saudi Arabia to help build a regional order capable of containing Iran. Israel wants Saudi normalization. Trump could use Riyadh to turn an expensive confrontation with Tehran into a strategic realignment of the Middle East.
Mohammed bin Salman, meanwhile, can afford to wait and see what everyone is prepared to offer.
Iran can raise oil prices. Saudi Arabia can still sell
Iran’s strategy depends partly on making the war economically painful far beyond the battlefield.
That makes the US an obvious target. Over Labor Day weekend, US gasoline prices were expected to average about $4.03 a gallon as renewed fighting pushed crude prices higher. With the midterm elections only weeks away, Tehran does not need to defeat Trump militarily. It needs Americans to feel the war every time they fill their tanks.
But there is a problem.
Iran can help make oil more expensive while increasingly struggling to sell its own. The US blockade has sharply reduced Iranian crude exports, with loadings falling from around two million barrels a day in March to roughly 220,000 to 255,000 barrels a day in August.
Saudi Arabia prepared for a different scenario.
For years, Riyadh invested in infrastructure designed to reduce its exposure to Hormuz. Its East-West Pipeline carries crude from the kingdom’s eastern fields to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing part of Saudi exports to bypass the strait.
That investment is paying off. The IMF found in July that rerouting crude through the pipeline helped limit the decline in Saudi oil deliveries, while higher prices more than compensated for lower volumes and produced an oil-revenue windfall.
The irony is hard to miss.
Tehran can make every barrel more valuable while losing the ability to sell enough barrels to fully benefit. Riyadh can still reach the market.
Iran’s energy weapon may be enriching the rival it was supposed to intimidate.
MBS built options before he needed them
Saudi Arabia’s advantage is not limited to pipelines.
For years, Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) has been building relationships designed to give Riyadh room to maneuver between competing powers.
Saudi Arabia deepened its economic relationship with China without abandoning its strategic partnership with Washington. More recently, Riyadh joined Turkey and Pakistan in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, adding another layer to a security strategy no longer built exclusively around the United States.
None of these relationships can replace Washington. The United States still offers military reach, intelligence, advanced weapons, and financial access that no other Saudi partner can match at the same scale.
But replacing America was never the point.
MBS does not need another America. He needs enough credible alternatives to make America compete for Saudi cooperation.
Iran is making that strategy more valuable.
The more dangerous the Gulf becomes, the more Washington needs partners capable of shaping what comes next. And few countries now occupy a more consequential position than Saudi Arabia.
Washington is no longer the only side setting the price
For years, the Saudi-Israel normalization debate revolved around what Riyadh wanted from Washington.
That is no longer enough to understand the negotiation.
The more important question is increasingly what Washington wants from Riyadh.
The United States wants Saudi weight behind a regional order that limits Iran. Israel wants normalization with the most important Arab state still outside the Abraham Accords. Trump wants an outcome he can present as something larger than another costly confrontation with Tehran.
All three roads run through Riyadh.
That changes MBS’s hand.
The proposed 30-year US-Saudi civilian nuclear cooperation agreement illustrates what is at stake. Washington has linked the deal to normalization with Israel, while Riyadh continues to demand meaningful movement on the Palestinian issue.
Iran’s pressure does not make those differences disappear.
It makes Saudi cooperation more valuable despite them.
The more indispensable Riyadh becomes to the regional architecture Washington wants, the harder it becomes to expect MBS to accept that architecture cheaply.
Iran may be creating Trump’s opening
Tehran’s strategy is supposed to trap Trump between two bad choices. Show restraint, and Washington risks looking unable to protect Gulf shipping and its regional partners. Escalate, and oil prices rise, Americans pay more at the pump, and the political cost grows at home.
But there is a third possibility: Trump could try to turn the Iranian threat into the argument for a much larger bargain with Saudi Arabia.
Washington and Jerusalem would get Saudi participation in a stronger regional framework and, potentially, normalization. Riyadh would seek the security commitments and strategic benefits it has wanted for years.
The Palestinian issue remains a major obstacle. So do the competing interests of all three governments. Nothing about such a bargain is inevitable.
But MBS has something increasingly valuable on his side: time.
He does not have to rush toward Washington, distance himself from China, or accept the first normalization package put in front of him. He can watch the pressure on the Gulf rise and ask a simple question: How much is Saudi cooperation worth now?
For years, Iran’s argument to its Arab neighbors rested on geography. America might eventually leave the Middle East. Iran would not. The Gulf states would therefore have to learn to accommodate Tehran.
Threatening Hormuz was supposed to reinforce that reality. It may be doing the opposite.
Every threat to Gulf shipping makes secure Saudi export routes more valuable. Every escalation makes Saudi cooperation more important to Washington. Every attempt to destabilize the regional order increases the country’s value, and everyone may need to rebuild it.
Iran wanted Riyadh to feel vulnerable enough to compromise. It may instead be making Riyadh indispensable enough to name its price.
Liron Rose is an entrepreneur, co-founder of the Masad Haaretz Institute, and creator and host of the geopolitical podcasts Israel Insider and HaYanshuf.
Amit Shabi is a former analyst in Intelligence Unit 8200, an investment and capital markets professional, author of several finance books, and a competitive chess player.

articles.title: Finland enters French-led European nuclear deterrence initiative
articles.body:
Finland has joined France’s European nuclear deterrence initiative, expanding defence cooperation with Paris while ruling out the stationing of nuclear weapons on Finnish territory in peacetime.
President Alexander Stubb said on Monday that the initiative was intended to strengthen European security, increase Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and reduce the risk of escalation.
Finland and France issued a joint statement confirming the decision after confidential talks at political and official level.
The initiative, launched by French President Emmanuel Macron in March, extends the European dimension of France’s nuclear deterrence. Finland becomes the tenth country to join, alongside Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Germany, Britain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Greece.
Stubb stressed that Finland would not host nuclear weapons in peacetime.
“There would be no sense in that,” he told reporters. He declined to speculate about possible arrangements during a war.
France will retain full control over its nuclear arsenal and will continue to decide what constitutes a threat to its vital interests. The initiative does not provide participating countries with a French nuclear umbrella or collective defence guarantees.
Finland’s main nuclear deterrence remains based on NATO and the extended deterrence provided by the United States, Stubb said.
The French initiative does not replace Nato’s nuclear deterrence and is not intended to duplicate it.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said Finland’s participation would deepen bilateral defence ties with France and strengthen national security.
“The French initiative is different from Nato’s nuclear deterrence,” Häkkänen said in a ministry statement. “The participating countries will not have obligations comparable to Nato’s collective defence.”
France is also not asking participating countries to contribute to the cost of maintaining its nuclear arsenal.
A joint working group will be established to define the practical forms of cooperation. Stubb said the process could last between 10 and 15 years.
Stubb said access to information about French nuclear deterrence was one reason Finland chose to participate.
He also said the involvement of Sweden, Norway and Denmark had influenced Finland’s decision, as the Nordic countries share security interests in northern Europe.
Russia has opposed the French initiative. Asked about Moscow’s likely response to Finland’s participation, Stubb said there was no need to overstate the situation.
“Keep a cool head,” he said.
The decision received broad parliamentary backing, according to Stubb, although the Left Alliance has said it opposes Finland joining the initiative.
The announcement comes as Finland and France expand defence cooperation in other areas. Stubb said France had already committed forces to activities in Finland and that the nuclear deterrence initiative added another element to the relationship.
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot are also due to sign a strategic partnership document in Helsinki on Monday.
HT

articles.title: Russia's new Geran drones changing air war in Ukraine — FT
articles.body:
LONDON, September 14. /TASS/. Russia’s upgraded Geran unmanned systems that can fly at a high speed and altitude have changed the air war in Ukraine, actually blurring the line between drones and cruise missiles, the Financial Times (FT) reported.
While the early-generation Geran-1 drone carries a warhead of up to 20kg and has a top speed of 185 km/h, the jet-powered Geran-5 drone can fly at up 600 km/h and carry a warhead of 90kg over a range of 1,000km, the FT wrote. According to it, the new drones are equipped with thermal cameras and targeting systems based on AI as well as anti-jamming antennas.
Centralized production has enabled the Russian side to "adapt the drones, absorb battlefield feedback and deploy new models quickly," the FT continued. "The drones cost a fraction of the missiles that formed the core of Moscow’s previous air campaigns," the newspaper reported, adding that "mass production has also accelerated innovation."

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 unmanned aerial vehicles, 85 of which were destroyed or suppressed by air defense
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 unmanned aerial vehicles, 85 of which were destroyed or suppressed by air defense
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 108 drones of various types at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 85 drones; impacts were recorded at seven locations.
During the night of September 14, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 108 strike drones of various types. Air defense forces destroyed and suppressed 85 enemy drones. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN writes.
Details
Starting in the evening of September 13, the occupiers used Shahed-type attack UAVs, including jet-powered ones, as well as Gerbera-type drones and Parody decoy drones.
The launches were carried out from the areas of Orel and Kursk in Russia, as well as from the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk region and Crimea — from the area of Hvardiiske.
The air attack was repelled by fighter aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense had destroyed or suppressed 85 enemy Shahed-, Gerbera- and other types of UAVs
At the same time, hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at seven locations.
The Air Force emphasized that the attack is ongoing. Enemy drones remain in Ukraine’s airspace.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia agreed to halt strikes on energy. Zelenskyy is not so sure.
articles.body:
KYIV — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has poured cold water on his American counterpart Donald Trump's claim that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure.
Trump over the weekend blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Moscow’s refineries — not the U.S.-Israel war on Iran — for high diesel prices, then on Monday said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt attacks on energy targets.
Ukraine, though, is skeptical. Russia has been barraging Ukraine’s ports, energy grid, fuel stations, and logistics with dozens of jet-powered drones and missiles for several years. The attacks, as well as Ukrainian counterstrikes on Russian infrastructure, have escalated in recent weeks.
Advertisement
“Ukraine is not confident that Russia has any intention of adhering to any agreement," Zelenskyy said in a post on X, indicating that Ukraine won't stop its attacks other than on a reciprocal basis.
If partners can "ensure Russia's genuine desire to refrain from striking our electricity, our other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, or the movement of food supplies, then we, of course, are ready to reciprocate with a corresponding absence of our own strikes," he wrote.
The Ukrainian leader claims that if there is a ceasefire, it must be long-term to be reliable, rather than a short-term deal allowing Russia to hold parliamentary elections on Sept. 18 - Sept.20. He said it must not be a tool to “secure a temporary easing of tensions over gasoline and diesel,” Zelenskyy said.
“We await specifics from our partners,” Zelenskyy added.
The Kremlin has not issued any comments on Trump’s announcement yet. Earlier today, its spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Trump’s call for Kyiv to stop attacks on “peaceful economic infrastructure," but refused to say whether Russia will stop bombing Ukraine’s infrastructure if Kyiv agrees.
Trump previously secured a three-day ceasefire in May, allowing Russia to hold Victory Day celebrations. On the same days, Moscow attacked Ukraine with 40 drones and a ballistic missile.

articles.title: Russia facing difficulties with Chinese jet engines for drones – Ukrainian intelligence agency, photo
articles.body:
Russia facing difficulties with Chinese jet engines for drones – Ukrainian intelligence agency, photo
Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Head of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), has said that Russia is experiencing problems with jet engines for drones. He said it during the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES) meeting in Kyiv.
Source: Interfax-Ukraine
Details: Skibitskyi said this was why international sanctions remained essential. He noted that Russia was currently facing certain difficulties obtaining jet engines for drones, specifically engines from China, and said this was the result of actions taken by Ukraine and its partners.
Skibitskyi also said that China was aware of the potential consequences, risks and problems for its own industry associated with supplying Russia.
Skibitskyi separately noted that Ukrainian intelligence was aware of all Russian companies involved in production, including joint manufacturing with Chinese companies.
He stressed, however, that these facilities were located far from Ukraine's border, at distances of more than 2,000 km. Striking such targets was difficult and could only be done using long-range strike capabilities, including drones, he added.
Background:
- Skibitskyi previously said that Russia was entirely dependent on supplies of Chinese turbojet engines for its Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones. At the same time, Russia is attempting to establish domestic production of such engines.
- According to DIU, one Chinese turbojet engine costs around US$40,000.

articles.title: Will strategic Marib hold the key to Yemen's conflict?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Will the strategic province of Marib hold the key to Yemen's conflict?
Amid the renewed fighting between Yemen’s Houthi rebels and government forces and the Houthis’ capture of the whole of the country’s Red Sea coast, there is increasing speculation that the oil-rich province of Marib will be the next major theatre of conflict.
For many years, Marib has served as an impenetrable barrier against the expansion of the Houthi movement. It is one of the last strongholds of the internationally recognised government in northern Yemen and occupies a strategically important position 120 kilometres east of the capital Sana’a, which was captured by the Houthis in 2014.
Government forces in the area have so far adopted a defensive strategy, but amid the renewed fighting, it could become a base for them to seize the initiative and launch offensive operations.
This strategic shift has already been reflected on the ground in recent developments. Last week, government forces announced the launch of a wide-ranging military operation to take control of Houthi-held areas of the province.
These included an intensive assault by units of the Seventh Military Region, which broke through Houthi defences and recaptured strategic positions northwest of Marib city, alongside a successful flanking operation in the Mahzam Mas area.
In the south, government forces also took control of the Al-Akad Al-Ramli area and positions near Mount Al-Balaq amid fierce fighting that resulted in many deaths and the capture of Houthi prisoners as well as the seizure of military vehicles.
These operations coincided with the Yemeni armed forces repelling two major attacks launched by the Houthis against military positions in the south and west of the province. 
The fighting was described as the most severe since 2021 and has marked the beginning of a new phase on the battlefield, in which the government is on the attack.
The government currently maintains full control over the province’s heartland and all its strategic points.
The tipping point of the Yemeni conflict
Marib is seen as the tipping point of the balance of power in Yemen – a key area on which the entire structure of the internationally recognised government rests.
It covers 17,478 square kilometres, with terrain ranging from rugged mountainous areas to vast desert plains.
Its population before the war was around 348,000, but around two million internally displaced people have fled there, living in hundreds of camps and shelters.
This places enormous pressure on its infrastructure and public services.
As the last major stronghold of the government in northern Yemen, it has become a key administrative centre where state institutions and military and security forces are concentrated.
Its survival is seen as key to the continuation of the Yemeni national project. 
Militarily, Marib is a highly complex and vital geographical hub. It forms a strategic link between Al-Jawf, Sanaa, Al-Bayda, Shabwa and Hadramawt province, while also acting as a fortress that has repelled some of the Houthis’ fiercest attacks. 
The fronts surrounding it have therefore become the first line of defence for Yemen’s east and south.
Financial and military lifeline
Economically, Marib is the country’s most important financial lifeline. It contains the major oil and gas fields in Safer, as well as a key power station, which supplies large areas of the country with electricity. It also generates sovereign revenues that finance a significant portion of state expenditure and essential services.
The military control map in Marib is characterised by considerable geographical complexity, with front lines intersecting and defensive and offensive positions overlapping between government forces and tribes on one side and the Houthi movement on the other.
While the government controls most of the province, including Marib city and the strategically important Al-Wadi district, the Houthis are present in peripheral mountain and desert areas, including areas bordering Al-Jawf governorate to the north and Al-Bayda and Shabwa governorates to the south and west.
This military overlap makes Marib an open front, with every possibility still on the table. Government forces are attempting to secure their security perimeter by taking control of  high ground in frontline districts, thereby cutting off potential routes for Houthi missile launches and ground attacks on the province’s population centres.
The potential military and strategic objectives of a government offensive appear clearly defined.
Military and political objectives
One major objective is to recapture the remaining districts under Houthi control, as well as secure and clear the western and northwestern areas bordering Sanaa and Al-Jawf. 
These areas have served for years as major launching platforms for missile and drone attacks against residential neighbourhoods and critical infrastructure in Marib city.
Government forces are supported by a paramilitary organisation called the Popular Resistance, made up of residents of Houthi-controlled governorates who have been displaced to Marib. 
Government-allied tribal fighters also constitute an active force, possessing heavy weapons and extensive knowledge of the terrain. 
On the Houthi side, the movement relies on mobilising ideological and regional military formations belonging to what it calls the “Central Military Region.” These are stationed at strategic camps that the Houthis have seized and converted into advanced offensive platforms.
The most prominent include Mas Camp in northwestern Marib, as well as the Tamah and Khashm Al-Jafina camps.
The Houthis rely heavily on a war of attrition, using an arsenal of ballistic missiles and drones to attack government positions.
Government camps and fronts constitute the final defensive shields protecting the population centres, economy and energy facilities, while Houthi camps serve as major launch bases for threatening the front lines and attempting to penetrate the defensive perimeter around Marib city.
If the government does manage to make major advances in Marib, taking control of some or all of the Houthi positions in the province, this would represent a major turning point capable of redrawing the map of Yemen’s conflict and altering the balance of power.
Politically, it would likely push the Houthis toward serious engagement with peace negotiations while militarily opening routes towards the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
Most importantly, it would constitute clear confirmation of the internationally recognised government’s ability to determine the outcome of the conflict and restore confidence in the Yemeni national project.

articles.title: ‘The Battlefield Has Gone Underground’: Khartiia Commander Reveals Ukraine’s Edge Over Russia
articles.body:
The battlefield in one sector of Ukraine’s front has moved underground, where Ukrainian troops are proving more effective than Russian forces, according to Ihor Oboliensky, commander of the National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps.
“Today, in our corps’ area of responsibility, the battlefield has gone underground,” Oboliensky, known by the call sign “Kornet,” said during the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“And we are more effective there than the Russians.”
Oboliensky, who holds Ukraine’s highest state honor, Hero of Ukraine, said the shift was another example of how rapidly the war is changing. Technologies and battlefield tactics that were relevant two years ago are now outdated, while new developments can alter combat operations every two or three months.
The commander said that constant adaptation is also reshaping Ukraine’s air-defense requirements, particularly as Russia develops faster jet-powered attack drones.
Despite the growing focus on aerial attacks and military technology, Oboliensky warned against shifting attention away from infantry and the front line.
“The soldier remains the most important. Please do not shift the focus under any circumstances,” he said.
Russia will continue striking Ukrainian cities as long as its forces can show progress on the battlefield, he said. Halting Russian advances and denying Moscow even small territorial gains would undermine the Kremlin’s justification for continuing the war.
Ukraine Sees Exponential Growth in Private Security Firms Providing Anti-Drone Protection
“As soon as the front is stopped, as soon as Moscow has no success, not a single kilometer, then you will ask the question, and Moscow and Putin will face the same question: Why are you fighting? Why are you not advancing?” Oboliensky said.
Areas for improvement
The commander identified three main areas in which Ukraine needs greater help from its partners: financing, access to technology and industrial capacity, and military training.
Western countries should help finance at least half of Ukraine’s available production capacity for drones and missiles, Oboliensky said, as such cooperation would support Western economies while also creating work for Ukrainians.
Oboliensky also described how Ukrainian officers serving under his command had traveled to France for training and visited the Normandy beaches, where Allied forces landed during World War II.
The officers called him by video from Utah Beach and said seeing the site had transformed their understanding of military logistics, he recalled.
“They said, ‘Commander, we understood what logistics means,’” Oboliensky said.
The visit demonstrated that success in battle depends not only on troops fighting at the front but also on the ability to deliver everything they need, he said.
Oboliensky spoke during a discussion with Ukrainian military commanders at the 22nd YES Annual Meeting, held in Kyiv on Sept. 11-12. The event brought together about 700 politicians, diplomats, military personnel, business leaders, veterans, activists, and experts from 28 countries, according to organizers.

articles.title: The situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a war | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.body:
“I will not send you to fight and die in stupid foreign wars that never end,” Donald Trump promised a crowd in Pennsylvania in 2024. While the disastrous conflict in Iran, which has escalated in recent days, may make it seem like the president has reneged on that promise, that’s inaccurate. It would be wrong to say that the president has dragged the US into yet another disastrous forever war in the Middle East because, as government officials keep insisting, what’s happening in Iran isn’t actually a war.
“I wouldn’t call it a war,” JD Vance told reporters early this month, for example, after being asked whether the fighting in Iran might be over by the November midterms. “Right now, there is no active shooting.”
Maybe not, but there has been quite a bit of active bombing. Earlier this month, a US missile strike hit a wedding at a private home in southern Iran, killing at least four people, including a four-year-old child and a 16-year-old. That’s fairly restrained compared to the massacre in March when a US precision-guided missile hit an elementary school in Iran, killing 150 people, including 120 children, but it’s still something I would personally file under “possible war crimes”.
But not only does the Trump administration keep insisting this isn’t a real war, they’re also adamant there aren’t any real crimes being committed: the vice-president would like to stress that you shouldn’t believe your eyes or ears when it comes to the civilian deaths being reported. Despite a weapons expert and a visual analysis by the New York Times concluding that the bomb that hit the wedding party in a residential area of the country was American, Vance has a hunch the whole thing might have been made up by some untrustworthy brown people.
“The Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far,” Vance said at that same press briefing, in relation to the wedding massacre. “So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”
The vice-president may be skeptical, but I’m confused. If this isn’t a war, what is it? A little skirmish? An interminable series of special military operations? A very bloody screw-up? Trump himself has called it a war on several occasions. Last Wednesday, for example, he said: “The war is going to end immediately after the election.” However, rather confusing matters, he also recently suggested he agreed with Vance that it wasn’t a full-fledged war. “I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us,” Trump said last month. Those are some very expensive potatoes: the not-a-war already has a price tag of tens of billions. Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, has roughly estimated that it has cost the typical US household $1,200. And then of course there’s the human cost: the thousands of lives that have been lost.
What we call this “military conflict” isn’t just semantics, it matters greatly. Not least because the constitution is very clear that a president can’t unilaterally start an official war on a whim; only Congress has the power to declare a war. Trump isn’t the first president to launch major military action without going to Congress for a declaration: Harry Truman classified the Korean conflict as a “police action” to bypass Congress and presidents since have engaged in similar semantic sleights-of-hand. But, as the historian and foreign relations expert Fredrik Logevall noted in an interview with the Harvard Kennedy School: “What’s extraordinary about President Trump in the current context is that he has not really bothered to even consult with Congress, never mind seek the approval of Congress.” In other words, he’s acting like a dictator.
Trump, to be fair, has been clear that he’s exploiting the Truman Playbook. “I won’t use the word ‘war’ because they say if you use the word ‘war,’ that’s maybe not a good thing to do,” Trump said at a fundraising dinner in March. “They don’t like the word ‘war’ because you’re supposed to get approval. So, I’ll use the word ‘military operation’, which is really what it is. It’s a military decimation.”
Avoiding a formal declaration of war might also help the US government bypass certain “wartime” obligations to its service members and their families. Libby Klinner, the widow of an airman killed in combat operations against Iran in March, recently posted on Instagram that she wasn’t receiving certain benefits because the US wasn’t technically at war.
“The Air Force recently told me that because we haven’t officially declared war, my kids and I aren’t eligible for some benefits,” Klinner wrote. “So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we’re left with are being dictated by semantics and public perceptions.”
After this post went viral, it seems the government has stepped in smooth things over. Vance recently said the administration would ensure Klinner receives “what she is entitled to.” He added: “We will certainly work that on the back end.”
The government might be able to fix Klinner’s benefits, but they’re going to have a hard time remedying the economic and political damage this not-a-war is inflicting. Trump’s popularity is plummeting, and a majority of Americans are fed up with this “small potatoes” conflict that has been going on for six months and making everyday life more dangerous and expensive. According to an estimate from Brown University last week, the conflict has cost Americans $100bn in extra energy costs. That bill is going up by $1m every two minutes. This week oil prices also climbed over $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
Meanwhile, with hostilities escalating and no off-ramp in sight, it looks like Trump is out of options. All he has left is empty promises. The president has insisted that energy prices will tumble “right after the election” and, in a sign he is completely desperate, promised every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November. The Trump administration can call the war whatever they like, but future generations will define it as a disastrous act of hubris.
- 
  Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: Ukrainian Armed Forces Tank Troops Day: the history of the holiday
articles.body:
Ukrainian Armed Forces Tank Troops Day: the history of the holiday
Kyiv • UNN
On September 14, Ukraine celebrates Tank Troops Day, established in 2023 instead of Tanker’s Day. Tanks remain important in the war of drones, and the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ fleet has been reinforced with Western-made vehicles.
Today, September 14, Ukraine celebrates Tank Forces Day. Despite the fact that modern warfare is increasingly being called a drone war, tanks and tank units have not lost their importance on the battlefield. Armored vehicles continue to perform important tasks - supporting infantry, striking enemy positions, covering units, and ensuring troop mobility. UNN explains why Ukraine changed the date of the tank crews’ professional holiday, what role tanks play in modern warfare, and how Ukraine’s armored vehicle fleet has changed over the years of the full-scale invasion.
Why Tankers’ Day was replaced with Tank Forces Day and when this happened
On September 9, 2023, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, "honoring the courage and heroism of tank crews demonstrated in the struggle for Ukraine’s freedom, independence, and territorial integrity, as well as with the aim of establishing new military traditions," established Tank Forces Day in Ukraine, celebrated annually on September 14.
Zelenskyy’s decree replaced a decree by Ukraine’s second President, Leonid Kuchma - No. 922/97, under which Tankers’ Day was celebrated annually in Ukraine on the second Sunday of September.
The modern date was established to honor the courage of Ukrainian tank crews and to launch a new military tradition. Symbolically, it was linked to the 2022 Kharkiv offensive, after which, on September 14, the Ukrainian flag was raised over liberated Izium.
The history of the holiday in Ukraine
The change was not merely formal. The new holiday was created as part of a Ukrainian military tradition linked to the modern history of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. It was on September 14, 2022, after the main phase of the Kharkiv offensive and stabilization measures had been completed, that the blue-and-yellow flag was raised over liberated Izium.
The Kharkiv counteroffensive became one of the most successful operations conducted by the Defense Forces during the first year of the full-scale war. Tank units ensured the high speed of advance and the firepower of Ukrainian forces. According to various reports, during this operation Ukrainian troops also captured 77 Russian tanks, some of which were later used against the occupying forces.
Thus, September 14 has a dual significance. It is a professional date for Ukrainian tank crews and, at the same time, a reminder of one of the operations that demonstrated the Defense Forces’ ability to conduct rapid mechanized offensives and liberate significant territories.
The role of tank units in modern warfare
War is changing faster than anyone can adapt. Drones, reconnaissance, and new tactics – all of this rewrites the rules every month. But one thing remains unchanged: when it is necessary to break through defenses or cover infantry on the ground, a tank goes there.
The war has changed, and so has the role of the tank on the battlefield. But the relevance of tank crews has not yet faded.
Tank forces remain one of the key elements of the ground forces even amid a war of drones, precision weapons, and advanced reconnaissance systems. Despite the changing nature of combat operations, armored vehicles continue to perform critically important tasks – from breaking through defenses to supporting infantry and deterring the enemy.
Ukraine’s tank forces remain an important element of modern warfare, combining mobility, firepower, and the ability to influence the course of combat operations. Their effectiveness today is determined not only by the technical characteristics of tanks, but also by the level of coordination with infantry, artillery, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare systems.
Understanding the role of tank forces makes it possible to better assess why armored vehicles continue to play a key role in the Armed Forces of Ukraine even amid a war of drones, where technologies are changing rapidly and adaptation is becoming a decisive factor in success.
Ukraine’s armored vehicle fleet
After 2022, the Ukrainian armored vehicle fleet became significantly more diverse. Before the full-scale invasion, the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s tank fleet consisted of Soviet T-64, T-72, and T-80 tanks of various modifications, but after 2022 Ukraine received Western main battle tanks from its partners.
T-64 model 2017 of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
The rearmament of Ukrainian crews with equipment built to different standards also became important. For example, in 2023, the United Kingdom transferred 14 Challenger 2 tanks to Ukraine, the United States announced the transfer of 31 M1 Abrams tanks, and Germany delivered the first 14 Leopard 2 tanks.
British Challenger 2 in service with the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Subsequently, the number of Western armored vehicles increased thanks to contributions from other partners.
American M1 Abrams fitted with Kontakt-1 explosive reactive armor
Poland contributed the most to replenishing the main battle tank fleet—more than 300 vehicles, including T-72, Leopard 2, and PT-91 Twardy tanks.
Leopard 2A4 of Ukrainian servicemen
As already noted, Ukraine’s tank fleet was predominantly a Soviet legacy. Ukrainian designers also did not stand still, creating the T-64BM Bulat, which is an upgrade of the Soviet T-64BV tank. The upgrade included strengthening the protection of the hull and turret with Nozh explosive reactive armor, a more powerful engine, and a number of other improvements.
T-64BM "Bulat"
Ukrainian designers also created one of the best modern tanks—the BM Oplot, developed by the Kharkiv Morozov Machine-Building Design Bureau. The BM Oplot is a fundamental modernization of the T-84 tank and the newest representative of the series.
BM "Oplot"

articles.title: Ukraine’s Flamingo Missile Blasts Russian Plant Linked to Iskander, Kinzhal and Kalibr Production
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Flamingo Missile Blasts Russian Plant Linked to Iskander, Kinzhal and Kalibr Production
Satellite imagery has confirmed significant damage to Russia’s Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant following a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile strike, with part of the facility’s main production building destroyed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Satellite images published by the Exilenova+ OSINT project show that one FP-5 missile struck the plant during an attack overnight on September 11, destroying a section of its main workshop measuring approximately 20 by 15 meters.
“One of the FP-5 missiles completely destroyed part of the main workshop measuring 20 by 15 meters,” Exilenova+ said.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, which produces the Flamingo missile, also confirmed the use of the FP-5 against the facility, according to Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka on September 13.
Fire Point said the strike destroyed an attached section of the building covering approximately 380 square meters.
“As a result of the hit, the building covering an area of about 380 square meters completely collapsed and was destroyed,” the company said. Exilenova+ also reported that another Flamingo missile apparently failed to reach the plant, with satellite imagery showing an impact crater near the facility.
Volgogradpromproekt is located in Volgograd’s Kirovsky district and specializes in small-scale chemical production, including organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants, resins, and other specialized industrial chemicals.
One of the company’s key products is OSF, an organosilicon derivative of ferrocene containing iron compounds. The substance is used as a catalyst and burn-rate modifier in composite solid rocket propellants, allowing manufacturers to regulate how quickly the propellant burns while maintaining required characteristics.
Volgogradpromproekt supplies Russian defense manufacturers, including the Perm Powder Plant, which produces propellants and explosives for more than 100 weapons systems, including Grad and Smerch rockets and surface-to-air missiles.
The plant has also been linked to production chains for Kalibr cruise missiles and air-launched anti-ship missiles. Another major customer, the Kamensky Chemical Plant, produces solid fuel for Iskander-M and Kinzhal missiles, as well as Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S rockets.
Volgogradpromproekt also supplies materials used in shipbuilding, including to the Amur Shipbuilding Plant, which builds Project 22800 Karakurt-class missile ships.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces used FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Russia’s Progress Rocket Space Center in Samara, the country’s only facility that serially assembles Soyuz-2 launch vehicles.

articles.title: Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones
A Russian Navy corvette stationed at Kronstadt has been painted to resemble a waterfront building and fitted with protective netting, as Moscow continues adapting its Baltic Fleet vessels against Ukrainian drone attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on September 14, photographs published by military observer Massimo Frantarelli show a Project 1331M corvette, known by NATO as the Parchim II class, with painted outlines resembling windows and doors across its hull. Netting has also been installed above parts of the deck as a physical barrier against incoming drones.
The vessel was photographed at the Leningrad Naval Base in Kronstadt on August 22. Frantarelli said the ship could be either the Zelenodolsk or Kazanets, although its exact identity has not been confirmed. Russia operates roughly six of the East German-built anti-submarine corvettes, each displacing about 800 tons.
The modified vessel is part of a broader effort to alter the appearance of Russian warships based at Kronstadt. Naval analyst H I Sutton has documented several Baltic Fleet ships using black-painted bows and sterns, checkerboard patterns, and other disruptive designs since mid-2026.
Two Project 22800 Karakurt-class missile corvettes, Mytishchi and Burya, were also seen in July with unusual paint schemes and anti-drone netting.
The measures followed successful Ukrainian strikes against Russian naval assets in the Baltic region. On June 3, Ukrainian forces struck the corvette Boikiy while it was undergoing work in dry dock at Kronstadt, causing significant fire damage. Ukrainian officials said the vessel may have been damaged beyond repair.
In March, Ukrainian drones also sank the Russian patrol ship Purga near Vyborg, northwest of St. Petersburg. According to Defence Blog, neither vessel had protective anti-drone netting installed when it was targeted.
Similar techniques have historical precedent. During World War Two, warships were sometimes painted to distort their outline or blend into nearby infrastructure. Germany’s battleship Tirpitz reportedly carried a scheme during fitting-out at Wilhelmshaven that included painted features intended to make the hull resemble buildings along the waterfront.

articles.title: Ukraine hit the radar that guards Sochi, the Russian resort city it struck ten days ago
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the 92N6 multifunction radar of a Russian S-400 Triumf air defense system in Sochi, the General Staff said on 14 September. The S-400 is Russia's longest-range air defense system. The radar tracks aerial targets and guides the system's missiles onto them, which makes it the part of an S-400 that decides whether the launchers can fire at anything. The strike came on 13 September and overnight into 14 September, alongside hits on drone launch sites, radars, and relays elsewhere in Russia and occupied Crimea, according to the military.
What was hit in Sochi
Ukrainian monitoring channels reported the explosions hours before the military did. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ published night footage from Sochi at 3:29 with the sound of small arms fire, drone engines, and an explosion in the air, then a second clip in which the blast came on the ground. At 4:25 the channel posted a clip of distant explosions in Dagomys, a suburb of Sochi.
Sochi's regional operational headquarters claimed that falling drone debris injured five people in the city, including a child, and that one adult went to hospital and three private houses took damage. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian drones overnight.
By 11:34, Exilenova+ reported that a new-generation medium-range air defense system and the infrastructure of a military unit near Dagomys had preliminarily been hit overnight.
Sochi is a Russian resort city on the eastern Black Sea coast, about 600 km from the front line in southern Ukraine. Drones hit two fuel depots there and an air defense position near the Abkhazia border on 4 September, and satellite imagery later showed nine destroyed storage tanks and impact marks at the air defense position, which Russian officials had never acknowledged.
The rest of the target list
Near Kursk and the occupied city of Donetsk, Ukrainian forces hit sites where Russia stores, prepares, and launches attack drones, the General Staff said. A drone control point of a Russian unit was struck in Novohrodivka, Donetsk Oblast.
Radar stations were hit in Litizh, Trostenchik, and Lipovka in Bryansk Oblast, and three signal relays in Rokhmanovo, Krasny Styag, and Kamen in the same oblast. At Saky airfield in occupied Crimea, Ukrainian forces struck a short-range radio navigation system.
The extent of the damage is being assessed, the General Staff said, adding that work against key Russian military targets continues.

articles.title: Polish authorities say they found a Russian drone on the country’s territory
articles.body:
A Russian drone washed up on a Baltic Sea beach in Rusinowo, near the Polish town of Jarosławiec, Poland’s Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
“A preliminary inspection indicates that this is a Russian military drone. Emergency services are working at the scene,” the minister said.
Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command stated that its systems had detected no violations of national airspace since July 31.
“Therefore, at this time, this incident cannot be linked to any attack by the Russian Federation,” the Polish news outlet PolsatNews quoted command spokesperson Jacek Goryszewski as saying.
Russian forces attacked a gas station near the Yahodyn border crossing and a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw railway line with drones overnight on September 13. Two people were injured in the strike on the gas station, Suspilne reported. No one was hurt in the strike on the train.
Afterward, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “escalation on the part of the Russian Federation is becoming a fact, and its examples are getting closer and closer to our [Polish] border.” In the coming weeks and months, the Polish prime minister believes, Russia will try to intensify its actions in Ukraine. “We cannot rule out, unfortunately, that this escalation will also affect our territory,” he said.

articles.title: Russia Launches Kalibr Cruise Missiles Directly From Base, Ukraine Says
articles.body:
Russia has been launching its naval-based Kalibr cruise missiles directly from port via its missile carriers for four months in a row, according to Ukraine.
Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk noted the new trend on television, according to state media Ukrinform on Monday, Sept. 14.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Even the use of cruise missile carriers that launch Kalibrs takes place directly at the base, that is, right in the harbor. This is a trend that has been observed for the fourth month in a row,” Pletenchuk said.
The Kalibr, with a reported range of 1,500-2,500 km (932-1,553 miles), is the mainstay in the Russian Navy’s arsenal and have been frequently used against Ukrainian cities since 2022.
The missiles are typically launched at sea by Russian warships and submarines, with Ukrainian channels closely monitoring their movements ahead of potential missile strikes.
Pletenchuk noted the peculiar nature and difficulty in launching them from the harbor, before warning that the missiles’ danger should not be overlooked.
“Submarines, for example, are also not so easy to use. To do this, they need to dive. I still can’t imagine how they can use them in the mode in which they are currently launching them,” Pletenchuk continued.
“Let’s not downplay the danger: we are assuming the maximum – four carriers, but realistic figures would probably be two surface carriers,” he added.
Canada Considers Joining EU €90 Billion Ukraine Loan
Pletenchuk also estimated that Russia has four vessels capable of launching the Kalibr missiles from the Black Sea – two Buyan-M-class warships and two Varshavyanka-class submarines.
On Sept. 9, Ukraine claimed to have hit the Admiral Essen, a Russian Admiral Grigorovich-class frigate capable of launching Kalibr missiles, at Russia’s Novorossiysk.
Pletenchuk also noted the decreased frequency of Russia’s cruise missile launches, saying that two had been documented this month, compared with a summer high of three.
Based on Kyiv Post’s tallies, Russia launched at least 251 cruise missiles in July, with massive strikes documented on three days (July 2, July 6, and July 30), where 40, 55 and 65 cruise missiles were launched, respectively, based on the Ukrainian Air Force’s morning updates.
The rest of July consisted of occasional cruise missile launches of up to 16 per day.

articles.title: Finland joins France’s nuclear deterrent initiative
articles.body:
Finland joins France’s nuclear deterrent initiative
- Finland has joined France’s Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative to strengthen European security amid concerns over US commitment and the Ukraine war.
- The initiative keeps French presidential authority over nuclear use but promotes joint exercises and potential deployment of nuclear-capable assets among partners.
- Finland follows Nordic countries joining earlier and emphasises the programme complements NATO without hosting nuclear weapons in peacetime.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – Finland has joined France’s initiative to extend the reach of its nuclear deterrent through collaboration with partner European countries, the heads of both countries said on Sept 14.
In response to US President Donald Trump’s expressions of concern about the US security commitment to Europe and to the security implications of the Ukraine war, France in March announced the Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative.
“The initiative is first and foremost about strengthening European security. It reinforces Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and helps prevent escalation,” Finland President Alexander Stubb said in a post on X.
Under the initiative, the French president alone has the authority to decide when nuclear weapons are used, in contrast to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which has a shared Nuclear Planning Group.
However, it offers joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Finland's defence minister Antti Hakkanen said in a separate statement that the agreement was a “natural step” following other Nordic countries, such as Norway, Sweden and Denmark, that joined the initiative earlier in 2026. In total, 10 countries participate, including Finland.
Stubb said the programme does not replace NATO’s nuclear deterrence and that Finland does not intend to allow nuclear weapons to be stationed on its territory in peacetime. REUTERS

articles.title: Fury after Russian strike on Ukraine train nearly catches dignitaries
articles.body:
European leaders expressed outrage Monday, a day after a Russian drone strike targeted a train near the Ukraine-Poland border, shortly senior visiting officials, including the former prime ministers of the U.K. and Sweden, passed through.
According to Ukrzaliznytsia, a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson, Carl Bildt and security advisers from several European Union states had purposely left the station at Yahodyn ahead of schedule. The visitors were on their way back from a security conference in Kyiv.
"It is highly probable that the Russian drone's intended target was in fact the diplomatic train, which had departed the station earlier than scheduled," the company said in a Telegram post.
Bildt, the former Swedish PM, shared a video on X of the attack at Yahodyn station, near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland.
"This wasn't our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing," Bildt said. "It was evacuated as the Russian drone approached and no one was hurt. Very good safety system. Our train just had an evacuation warning."
Bildt, Johnson and fellow passengers had been in Kyiv for the Yalta European Strategy conference, which is an annual gathering of leaders and experts across politics, business, security and media.
Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to Ukrzaliznytsia.
There were no immediate reports of casualties on any of the trains.
Ukrzaliznytsia said it "constantly adjusts train schedules" to guard against strikes.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Monday that Russian drone strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border would drive the military alliance to increase its support for Kyiv, calling the attacks on Sunday a sign of growing desperation by the forces under Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The strikes yesterday on trains in Ukraine close to NATO territory again show Putin's desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror," Rutte said at NATO's political headquarters in Brussels. "Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine."
Rutte pledged to increase support for Ukraine and bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defenses along its long eastern border with Russia.
"He thinks that he can stop us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong," the NATO chief said of Putin.
Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said Monday that the drone attacks near Poland's border were "clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine."
"We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared," she said.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Monday that Russia seeks to "divide" and "intimidate" Kyiv's European allies after a drone attack near a train carrying European officials in Ukraine.
"These attacks have a very clear objective: to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and, above all, divide them," Barrot told reporters on the sidelines of the European Arctic Summit in Finland.
He pointed out that the strikes occurred "as Ukraine was hosting a major economic support forum, attended by a large number of business representatives and diplomatic officials from around the world, particularly from Europe," according to broadcaster BFMTV.
Meanwhile, the office of U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that Russian strikes were aimed at undermining international support but Britain would not be deterred.
A spokesperson for his Downing Street office told journalists that the attack "was a futile attempt by Russia to undermine our support for Ukraine. It will not deter us."

articles.title: Trump Claims Ukraine, Russia Agreed to Halt Energy Infrastructure Strikes
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Monday, Sept. 14, that Ukraine and Russia agreed to halt strikes on each other’s energy infrastructure.
“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do so, likewise,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social media, while again pinning the blame for rising diesel prices on Ukraine’s targeting of Russian refineries instead of the US war in Iran.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv Post has reached out to Ukraine’s Presidential Office for comments but has not received a response at the time of publication.
In a statement issued an hour after Trump’s post, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv is ready to halt its strikes on Russian infrastructure, but only if Ukraine’s partners can ensure Moscow genuinely stops attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure.
“Every day, Ukrainian energy facilities, port infrastructure, logistics, and even warehouses storing food and pharmaceuticals are targeted,” Zelensky said, adding that “Ukraine is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by any agreement.”
Zelensky said that any agreement must be reliable, long-term and produce a tangible benefit for civilians, warning against a temporary deal that could collapse after Russia’s State Duma elections on Sept. 18-20.
He also pointed to short-term relief from pressure on Russia’s gasoline and diesel supplies.
Ex-CIA Chief: Inside Putin’s Mafia State
Zelensky concluded that “a de-escalatory step regarding critical infrastructure could be the first step toward peace.”
In an interview with Axios on Monday, Sept. 7, Zelensky said that Washington’s approach appeared to combine efforts to revive formal negotiations with informal measures aimed at preventing escalation over the winter.
He also said Kyiv intended to use the coming months to maintain diplomatic momentum.
Trump’s statement came a day after he publicly urged Zelensky to stop attacks on Russian diesel facilities, arguing that such strikes were contributing to a global diesel shortage.
The Kremlin welcomed the call but did not say whether Russia would halt attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure in return, according to Reuters.
“Any call on the Kyiv regime to stop attacks on civilian economic infrastructure can only be welcomed,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a daily conference call with reporters on Monday.

articles.title: FACTBOX: Russian strikes hit Kievstar mobile provider building, railway facilities
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. Russian strike drones hit the Kievstar mobile provider’s building, which also provides services to Ukraine’s military, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
Russian forces also hit locomotives and military trains carrying supplies for Ukraine’s army in the Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, Poltava, Nikolayev, and Odessa regions.
TASS has compiled the key details of the strikes.
Targets in the Kharkov and Sumy regions
- Russian pilots used aerial bombs and X-39 missiles to hit temporary deployment sites and drone command posts in the communities of Fyodorovka in the Kharkov Region and Zemlyanoye in the Sumy Region, respectively.
- The Defense Ministry released footage showing the strikes.
- Russian Aerospace Forces crews carried out the strikes using FAB-500 500-kilogram guided aerial bombs equipped with universal planning and correction modules, as well as two LMUR Kh-39 long-range air-launched missiles.
Railway transport
- Russian forces used Geran-4 Seeker strike drones to hit locomotives and military trains in the Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, Poltava, Nikolayev, and Odessa regions.
- The trains were used to carry various military supplies across Ukraine.
Strike on Kievstar building
- Russian drone operators from the Varyag Separate Brigade of Unmanned Systems carried out a precision strike on the Kievstar building in Ukraine.
- Kievstar is a telecom company providing mobile and internet services to Ukraine’s military.
Strike on gas station in Kiev
- Drone operators from the Varyag Brigade used a Geran strike drone to hit a gas station in Kiev.
- The gas station was used to serve Ukraine’s military, including its command, the Defense Ministry said, releasing footage of the strike.
Ukrainian unmanned boat assembly facility
- Russian forces hit a facility for assembling Ukrainian unmanned boats in the settlement of Grigorovka with a drone.
Situation in Ukraine
- Power outages were reported in the Dnepropetrovsk, Sumy, and Kharkov regions after energy infrastructure was damaged, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry reported.
- Some residents in the three regions were left without power.
- The ministry urged Ukrainians not to use high-power electrical appliances in the evening to prevent grid overloads.
- Electricity supplies were cut off in Kiev-controlled Kherson, the city’s head of the administration appointed by Ukrainian authorities, Yaroslav Shanko, reported.
- According to him, specialists are working to determine the cause of the power outage.

articles.title: Ukraine keeps hitting the fuel that Russia’s war runs on. Its latest target is the Slavyansk-EKO refinery, with an annual processing capacity of at least 3 million tonnes
articles.body:
An oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban in southern Russia was attacked overnight on 13 September, Astra reported. By morning, residents began posting videos showing smoke over the refinery and nearby areas. That same morning, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) reported that Ukrainian drones had struck the Slavyansk-EKO refinery.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have become systematic, aimed in part at reducing the Russian military’s access to fuel, which is critical for waging the war. Ukrainian forces have been striking strategic facilities located hundreds of kilometers from the front line.
The design capacity of Slavyansk-EKO is approximately 5.2 million tonnes per year, though actual volumes are lower by about one to two million tonnes, Militarnyi reports.
Thick smoke visible for dozens of kilometers
The Ukrainian strike hit a key oil-processing unit and the facility’s oil storage tank farm, which “fuels the criminal war against Ukraine,” HUR reported.
Two oil storage tanks were destroyed in the strike, according to photos published by Dnipro Osint. Militarnyi noted that the photos also show damage to neighboring tanks.
The strike reportedly hit the area containing the facility’s largest storage tanks. The refinery operates using purchased or tolling crude oil because it does not have its own crude oil production base.
The refinery has been targeted before
Slavyansk-EKO is one of the largest independent oil refineries in southern Russia. The facility is located in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, about 69 kilometers northwest of Krasnodar.
Ukraine’s General Staff said that the refinery is “part of the energy rear of the Russian Federation and involved in supplying the armed forces of the aggressor.”
Before the 13 September strike, Ukrainian drones had struck the refinery at least four times, starting in 2024:
- 27 April 2024 — a Ukrainian drone attack damaged the Slavyansk refinery, after which a fire broke out at the facility.
- 19 May 2024 — SBU drones attacked the Slavyansk refinery, after which the facility suspended operations.
- 26 January 2026 — Ukrainian Defense Forces struck infrastructure at the Slavyansk-EKO refinery. According to preliminary data, elements of the primary oil refining unit were damaged.
- Five months later, on 28 June, Ukraine struck the Slavyansk refinery again, causing a large fire at the facility. EP noted that the refinery supplies fuel, including to occupied Crimea.
