articles.title: “Fairly disciplined workers”: Russia’s prison service is replacing penal colonies with forced labor centers — and making money from it
articles.body:
As the military recruitment of prisoners reduces the population of penal colonies across Russia, the country’s Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) is expanding another branch of its system: correctional centers for convicts sentenced to forced labor. By the end of 2025, Russia had created 400 of these centers, with space for up to 50,000 people. This past June, FSIN even unveiled a “quickly deployable” center that can be installed directly at businesses nationwide. The new system is more profitable than traditional penal colonies, providing FSIN with fresh revenue streams and companies with access to a workforce almost entirely devoid of rights.
You’re not prisoners, but you can’t leave
Russian law does not classify forced labor as imprisonment, but a person sentenced to forced labor is nevertheless obligated to live in a closed FSIN facility. They must work wherever the administration sends them and cannot freely leave the correctional center.
“You can sit there and not go anywhere for a year,” Olga [name changed], a former convict who spent time in correctional centers from Perm to Volgograd, told The Insider. After a penal colony, Olga said, a correctional center can genuinely feel “almost like home.” People there can wear their own clothes, use a phone, read the news online, and communicate with relatives every day through messaging apps. But the relative improvement in quality of life that Olga experienced only applies to those who have previously spent time in a penal colony, where prisoners must wear standardized uniforms, communication with relatives usually happens by letter, and phones are banned.
For someone sent to a correctional center directly from life outside prison, the experience looks different: living by a schedule set by the FSIN, leaving the center only with permission, working forced overtime, and being subject to the administration’s will.
“People who were sent to a correctional center straight from home were somewhat shocked,” Olga recalled.
“A model correctional center with a sports ground and park”
According to Olga, life becomes especially hard when a correctional center is set up directly at a production site — with a dormitory next to the workshop and the employer working together with the administration to reduce inmates’ lives to moving between bed and the workplace. That is exactly the model FSIN now wants to replicate: fast-deployable correctional centers that can be built next to enterprises.
“At the St. Petersburg International Legal Forum, FSIN presented a model correctional center with a sports ground and a park. The project was sent to the regions as a recommendation,” TASS wrote in late June. In FSIN photographs, the model does not look like a prison but like a tidy workers’ dormitory: a long two-story modular building, lawns, bushes, streetlights, a separate sports ground, and a walking area with benches.
The TASS report also listed other elements of the project: a parking lot, a diesel power station, a transformer substation, and a separate yard where those who have violated prison rules can still get a chance to walk. But the presentation itself showed that the most attractive parts of the image — the park and sports ground — aren’t mandatory. A FSIN representative clarified that they are only “optional facilities.”
In other words, what was sent to the regions was not a plan for a center with a park but an easily replicable solution for quickly housing people sentenced to forced labor. The FSIN website describes it even more directly: the facilities can be built quickly “at any enterprise,” and the project can be used by representatives of large and medium-sized businesses interested in creating dormitories for convicts at their facilities.
That detail is crucial, Olga explained. She served her sentence both in a correctional center where she had to walk down the street to get to work and in a center where the dormitory was effectively on the production site.
“If it’s a closed-system correctional center, then the employer works in very close coordination with FSIN. No one’s getting away from them. FSIN plays the way the employer needs it to,” Olga said.
Employers work in very close coordination with FSIN in closed-system correctional centers
In that model, a person does not simply live near work — work becomes an extension of the prison regime.
“The conditions were always more lenient where the employer wasn’t in the same building as the dormitory. But where you live right in the workshop, right at the production site, that was where things were the hardest,” Olga recalled.
At one correctional center in the Moscow region, Olga said, the living quarters resembled a hangar or garage, with a workshop on the floor below. The facility had poor ventilation and was plagued by dirt, rats and cockroaches.
“It's legalized slavery,” she said. “They force people to work and use every tool of pressure and punishment available to make sure they keep working and don’t complain.”
30,000 workers with no rights
Forced labor as a new type of criminal punishment began to be used on Jan. 1, 2017, when FSIN opened its first four correctional centers and seven sections attached to its penal colonies, with a total capacity of fewer than 900 people. The first convicts arrived in March of that year. Now, a small network of facilities that was previously being tested as an alternative to colonies has turned into a separate and growing branch of the penal system.
By the end of 2025, according to FSIN Director Arkady Gostev, Russia had created 400 correctional centers and sections operating as correctional centers, with capacity for 50,000 people — and more than 30,000 convicts were actually being held there.
Given the overall decline in Russia’s prison population, those figures are especially notable. In May 2026, Gostev said that since the end of 2021 the number of people in places of detention had fallen from 465,000 to 282,000. About 85,000 of them were held in pretrial detention centers (SIZO) and PFRSI, a Russian abbreviation for facilities operating as pretrial detention centers, leaving about 197,000 in penal colonies and prisons.
The rise of correctional centers, whose inhabitants are not counted among the country’s prison statistics, do not explain that decline. Instead, the main reason for the drop in the population of penal colonies was the recruitment of prisoners for the war in Ukraine — first by the Wagner private military company, then by the Defense Ministry. In May, FSIN itself acknowledged for the first time that “efforts to recruit contract soldiers” for the armed forces was affecting the number of prisoners.
But at the same time, the agency is expanding the part of the system that is formally not considered imprisonment — exploiting the labor of convicts rather than simply isolating them away from society. The more than 30,000 people actually held in correctional centers already amount to about 15% of the current number of people under FSIN’s jurisdiction. The centers’ total capacity — 50,000 places — is comparable to about a quarter of that population.
The agency is expanding the part of the system focused not on isolation, but on exploiting convicts’ labor
At the same time, legal changes are making it easier to fill correctional centers. Since 2026, forced labor can be imposed as a standalone punishment, without a prior sentence involving imprisonment. The penalties under dozens of articles of the Criminal Code have also been expanded to include forced labor.
A “dormitory” behind a fence: What life is like in a correctional center
Russia’s Penal Enforcement Code describes correctional centers as special institutions for people sentenced to forced labor. They can exist separately, as sections attached to penal colonies, or directly at enterprises that use convict labor. Inside such centers, internal rules apply, and convicts are kept under supervision.
In correctional centers, people are allowed to have money, wear ordinary clothes, use a phone, access the internet, and keep personal belongings. At the same time, a convict must remain on the correctional center’s grounds, they may not leave without permission from the administration, they must carry an ID card at all times, they must follow internal rules, and they must take part in unpaid maintenance and improvement work for up to two hours a week. The person and the room where they live may be searched, and their belongings may be inspected. In effect, it is the same kind of closed institution as a penal colony, only with a softer internal regime.
The word “dormitory,” which is used to describe the living quarters in correctional centers, says little about the real conditions. Russia’s Penal Enforcement Code uses the same word for the places where convicts live in general-regime, strict-regime, and special-regime colonies. In practice, these are usually not separate rooms for a few people but buildings divided into large sections, each housing several dozen people. Even in the model FSIN showed at the St. Petersburg International Legal Forum, a large room with rows of beds can be seen inside the modular building. It looks more like a barracks-style sleeping hall than a regular dormitory.
Olga said conditions varied widely by region. In some places, the administration turned a blind eye to the rules, while in others, it used them as a tool of pressure. Still, the routine in forced labor facilities, she said, resembled the “Groundhog Day” rhythm of life in a penal colony:
“Wake-up, breakfast, go to work, a little lunch at work, and then at around 8 or 9 p.m. we come back from work, wash, have a bite to eat, and go to sleep. That’s basically every day.”
In some correctional centers, Olga said, people could go into town for a few hours on weekends. However, on others, people had to go months without leaving the grounds.
“If there are no problems, if the employer does not say they are working badly, then everything goes normally,” she said. “But if someone starts, for example, filing complaints against the employer, then the administration first of all restricts outings.”
Grigory Mumrikov, an artist who served a forced labor sentence in Zelenograd, just outside Moscow, after being convicted of participating in the organization of an anti-war protest, shared similar impressions. Compared with pretrial detention, the correctional center seemed to him like “great happiness,” even if he was still in captivity. From evening to morning, he was in the correctional center, and from morning to evening, he worked as a laborer at Aksakovo, a sanatorium run by FSIN. Mumrikov spent the couple of free hours he had after work walking around a lake.
“I could simply sit on a bench, just to avoid being on that territory,” he said, referring to the correctional center.
That was possible because the convicts worked outside the correctional center and traveled to and from Aksakovo on their own. But by 8 p.m., Mumrikov had to return to the center for the evening roll call.
“Everyone was rounded up and told to work weekends”
Under the law, people sentenced to forced labor must work wherever the correctional center’s administration sends them. Formally, their labor is supposed to be regulated by labor law. But convicts do not have the key right of a free worker: the right to refuse a particular job and leave for another employer.
Convicts do not have the key right of a free worker: the right to refuse a particular job and leave for another employer
In some correctional centers, Olga said, there was still some choice — the administration could offer two or three potential employers, and the person would choose where to work based on their skills and health. But that was not the case everywhere. In the correctional center in Leninsk, in the Volgograd region, where she was held in the winter of 2023-2024, there was only one employer: a canned goods factory.
“You cannot refuse to work, because that is considered a malicious violation,” Olga said.
According to her, people worked 10 to 12 hours a day, and weekends could be turned into workdays. However, if inspections began, the employer would show a normal schedule.
“The employers drew up a good schedule and pretended that no one had been forced to come in on weekends and that the working day was what it should be,” she said. “Accordingly, as soon as the inspectors leave, everything goes back to the way it was: longer working days and mandatory weekend work.”
The order to work on weekends, she said, usually came not directly from FSIN but from the production site. A foreman would gather the convicts, make sure no one had phones to record the conversation, and then announce the new schedule: “We work on weekends. We work until such-and-such time. And whoever complains will make things worse for themselves.”
That is what makes a convict’s position in a correctional center fundamentally different from that of an ordinary worker. In a correctional center, an employer’s demand almost automatically becomes an FSIN demand. The administration begins applying pressure, and complaints or refusal to work can result in disciplinary penalties.
“Inspectors work in coordination with the employer. They are one single system,” Olga said. If a person refuses to work for pennies or complains about conditions, she said, the administration can begin “catching them on small things” to find grounds for punishment. Accumulating such penalties creates the risk of transfer to a penal colony.
“Inspectors work in coordination with the employer. They are one single system”
Similar complaints have emerged in other regions. In Zelenograd, convicts in a correctional center said they worked without a proper schedule, faced overtime, and were threatened with tougher conditions if they reminded officials of their rights.
“We differ from undocumented migrants on a construction site only in that we are Russian,” forced laborers said.
Konstantin, a former prisoner who served his sentence in Kabardino-Balkaria in Russia’s north Caucasus, told the independent outlet Cherta that he was sent to sort household waste — eight hours in the heat at a rural dump that included hides of slaughtered cows and sheep, a terrible smell, large numbers of insects, and no ability to refuse the work.
Another person interviewed by the outlet, from the Voronezh Region in central Russia, worked at an agricultural complex growing mushrooms and said regular hired employees earned significantly more than convicts got from the correctional center.
These examples do not mean that people in every correctional center are forced to work overtime or are sent to the hardest jobs. Former convicts themselves also describe centers with decent working conditions and normal schedules. But all cases have one thing in common: a person cannot resign if they are unhappy with the conditions.
There is pay, but people support themselves
Officially, labor in correctional centers is paid. In any sentence, between 5% and 20% of a convict’s salary is withheld for the state, and the inmate is free to use the rest of the money. But unlike a penal colony, where prisoners have to be fed and issued uniforms, people in correctional centers are almost entirely self-supporting.
Convicts are given a bed and bedding, but they usually buy their food, clothes, shoes, hygiene products, medicine, and other everyday items while also reimbursing the correctional center each month for utilities and household services.
In Leninsk, in the Volgograd Region, Olga said, about 3,000 to 4,000 rubles ($35-$46) were withheld from her wages for utilities, and after all the deductions were made, convicts were typically left with about 9,000 to 10,000 rubles ($104-$116) a month to live on.
“And you have to take into account that this is not a colony: you need to dress yourself and eat something, because not all correctional centers provide food,” she said.
“This is not a colony: you need to dress yourself and eat something, because not all correctional centers have food”
Formally, if a convict has no money, the correctional center has to provide them with food, clothing, and shoes at the state’s expense. But in practice, Olga said, getting that support can be difficult.
“You go to the management and say: I have nothing to eat, you are supposed to provide me with food. And they say: ‘Well, where am I going to get it? You can see there is no kitchen,’” she said, describing life at a correctional center in the Moscow Region.
At the same time, Olga stressed that low pay is not an inevitable feature of correctional centers. In the Perm Region, where she worked at a private garment factory, the business was properly organized, and convicts’ wages could be comparable to ordinary wages outside the prison.
Olga earned about 40,000 to 50,000 rubles ($460-$580), while women who sewed well made up to 100,000 ($1,160), even after the deductions. “It was a fairly good place,” she said.
That contrast shows that the problem with correctional centers is not simply that they always pay poorly. With a decent employer, convicts can earn close to what they would outside prison. But if the employer is dishonest, the fact that a person is trapped means they are forced to survive on less than the national subsistence minimum.
What can lead to punishment in a correctional center
Under the Penal Enforcement Code, violations committed by people serving forced labor can lead to them being placed in an internal isolation cell inside the correctional center for up to 15 days. Olga said anyone sent there can only bring a minimum of belongings, and there is a ban on phones. “Not as frightening as in a colony, but the point is the same — to isolate you and show what they can do to you,” she explained.
The law separately defines “malicious violations,” which include refusal to work, disobeying the administration, participating in a strike or collective disobedience, possessing banned items, leaving the center without authorization, or returning more than 24 hours late. If a person is declared a malicious violator — for one “malicious” violation or for three ordinary violations within a year — the head of the correctional center submits a request to a court to transfer the person to a colony.
In practice, Olga said, these rules become a method of control. The administration may ignore minor violations for a long time, then use them against those who complain about an employer or refuse to work in poor conditions.
“They may treat you relatively well for a long time, but once you start demanding your rights, they begin finding fault with everything you do,” she said.
“Once you start demanding your rights, they begin finding fault with everything you do”
An everyday minor infraction can thus become part of a chain that ends in a person being packed off to a penal colony. “For those who came from a colony, that's the main fear,” Olga said. “They tell you: ‘if you don't want to work, you'll go back.’”
Who benefits from the new system
In public statements, FSIN describes correctional centers as a more humane alternative to colonies: a person is not completely isolated from society, and they can work, earn a salary, use a phone, and gradually return to normal life. In an explanatory note to the law expanding the use of forced labor, its authors wrote that such punishment allows convicts to maintain social ties, restore work skills, and compensate victims.
But this humanization also has an economic aspect. Under the Penal Enforcement Code, sections of correctional centers can be created directly at enterprises that use convict labor. The standard contract between a correctional center and a company describes the arrangement as a ready-made production scheme: the correctional center sends convicts, and the organization agrees to employ them at its site and report violations of labor discipline to the administration.
For businesses, this means access to workers whose minimal privileges depend on their successful fulfillment of assigned tasks. A convict cannot simply quit and leave for another employer, and as a FSIN representative told TASS, commercial entities are interested in creating such sections because people sentenced to forced labor are “fairly disciplined workers.”
“They are interested in doing their work well, because if they violate labor discipline or the procedure and conditions for serving their sentence, there is a risk that the punishment will be replaced with a harsher one — imprisonment,” the representative said.
The state additionally encourages businesses to take part in the scheme. Since 2026, organizations have been exempt from property tax on premises, territories, and other real estate they provide free of charge to house correctional centers.
The model is also convenient for FSIN. The agency does not need to build a traditional penal colony, as businesses provide part of the infrastructure while paying convicts enough that the state is not obliged to provide them with food, clothes, or medicine — 5% to 20% of their wages also go directly to the state.
In the end, businesses get workers whose discipline is backed by FSIN, while the agency gets infrastructure and a “contingent” — the official bureaucratic term used for prisoners and other people under state supervision — whose burden of support can largely be shifted onto the convicts themselves. At the same time, for FSIN and the state as a whole, this is a form of punishment that can be presented as humane resocialization.
A Gulag without isolation
The idea of correction through labor is not a new concept in the Russian penal system. In Soviet times, it was reflected even in the names of institutions, as camps and colonies were called “corrective labor institutions.” Soviet Russia’s Corrective Labor Code explicitly said that punishment should “correct and reeducate” convicts “in the spirit of an honest attitude toward labor.”
Under Stalin, this logic reached its extreme: the Gulag was not only a system of isolation and terror but also a vast economic mechanism. Prisoners built canals, railways, industrial facilities, and urban infrastructure. But direct comparisons between modern correctional centers and the Gulag would be misleading because the scale, conditions and level of violence are vastly different. Today, supervision is as light as possible, as it is the system itself that stimulates the efficiency of the inmates’ labor.
Correctional centers look like an updated version of the Soviet tradition of forced labor — without the barracks of the Gulag, but with the same basic idea that a convict must work for the benefit of the state — and now for Russia’s business sector
The state does not need to fully isolate a person in order to control them. It is enough to link their place of residence, their type of work, their salary, and the threat of transfer to a penal colony into a single system. As a result, correctional centers look like an updated version of the Soviet tradition of forced labor — without the barracks of the Gulag, but with the same basic idea that a convict must work for the benefit of the state — and now, also, for Russia’s business sector.
Not humanization, but a pragmatic move by FSIN
Correctional centers may offer better conditions than penal colonies, but they are still a form of deprivation of liberty, no matter what the paperwork says. In the end, they create even more opportunities to exploit prisoner labor than colonies do, and FSIN directly describes people sentenced to forced labor as a convenient labor resource.
Putin’s war in Ukraine is draining prisoners from Russia’s penal colonies, and dozens of institutions have closed down due to the lack of inmates. That could have led to FSIN losing bureaucratic influence (and with it, staff and funding from the state budget). Instead, the agency’s leadership appears to have found an effective way out: it can now report growth in the number of institutions providing a more humane form of punishment, and it can do so in a way that certainly pleases Russian businesses.

articles.title: Daily Code Drops at 30,000 Feet: How New Software Rules Could Help Munitions
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Defense industry leaders say the Air Force needs to be able to update the software on its munitions multiple times a day, not every few months, and a new Pentagon instruction released last week could enable that.
The instruction, titled “Accelerated Mission Software,” went into effect Sept. 8 and mandates that Pentagon acquisition offices use agile models for software acquisition and testing like development, security, and operations, or DevSecOps.
Speaking Sept. 14 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Rise8 CEO Bryon Kroger said the war in Ukraine have shown that the current model, where munitions technicians might wait months or longer to update software, doesn’t work on the modern battlefield.
“I don’t think that it’s a foreign concept to anybody in this room, but when it comes to software, we’ve just historically been bad at this,” said Kroger, a former USAF intelligence officer and cofounder of Kessel Run, the service’s first software factory. “In some cases, we’re fielding software slower than hardware.”
That slowness has often been the result of software not being prioritized during a weapon’s development, testing, and deployment—creating a challenge for Airmen in the field.
“You wouldn’t think about not establishing a refueling apparatus for aircraft that need it across long distances, but we haven’t really thought about, from an enterprise IT perspective, how to create a similar refueling apparatus, right?” Kroger said.
Pointing to Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s invasion, he called static software “dangerous at this point.”
“We end up talking a lot about hardware and stockpiling everything from munitions to rockets,” Kroger said. “But the question I’d add in the mix is whether the systems can change after we field them.”
The new Pentagon instruction could set the stage for faster software updates. It modernizes software practices such as built-in cybersecurity features, zero trust architecture, continuous testing, and software reuse before introducing new code.
The instruction bolsters software’s prominence by making its development and deployment a strategic asset across the DOD and establishes continuous monitoring across industry to manage supply chain risk.
It also sets rules to manage AI integration and maintain various validations for AI-generated code to protect government data.
The new rules for software development and deployment are based around how the commercial tech industry operates. Kroger made the case that the Pentagon and defense contractors need to follow commercial tech’s lead by decoupling software development cycles from hardware cycles—like how smartphone makers release software updates in between new phone models.
“And we need to set the bar high” Kroger said. “I hear people talking about, ‘Oh, it’d be really nice to get monthly software updates.’” Instead, he argued for updates multiple times a day to “get an update to the field on demand as soon as we need.”
Kroger said the software is critical to the service’s goal of growing its stockpile of munitions, which could become obsolete if the weapons don’ have the proper software to evolve with changing threats.
“The thing the commander actually needs to know isn’t just inventory,” Kroger said. “It’s those effects and both knowing the effects and producing them.”
Ursa Major CEO Chris Spagnoletti echoed Kroger’s comments on speeding up the software update and integration process with munitions hardware.
“When you mentioned software updates, I used to be an avionics guy years ago. The hairs on my back, my neck went up just because it’s so painful,” Spagnoletti said. “… When you make a software change, you have to do this battery of massive testing to make sure that you didn’t screw something else up.”
What’s key, he said, is to push boundaries on how to do the software work faster, while still maintaining the safety and rigor of the current process.

articles.title: Rumors of another mobilization have pushed some Russians from contingency plans to packed bags. Readers tell Meduza where they’ve fled.
articles.body:
Rumors of another mobilization have pushed some Russians from contingency plans to packed bags. Readers tell Meduza where they’ve fled.
Meduza recently asked readers who had decided to leave Russia in recent months to tell us how they found the courage to take such a difficult step. We wanted to know more than why people were leaving the country in 2026. The reasons clearly include the economic crisis, Internet restrictions, Ukrainian drone attacks, and rumors of possible mobilization. Above all, we wanted to know whether Russia was experiencing a genuine new wave of emigration. Judging by the number of letters our newsroom received, the answer is yes. Here are some of the most compelling stories you sent us.
Warning: This article contains adult language.
Alexey
Fryazino, Moscow region
I consider the mobilization rumors entirely credible, so I’m urging friends who are staying in Russia to gather medical records documenting their health problems — whether it’s a knee wrecked playing soccer or a patched-up skull from being hit by a flying board.
I had been thinking about moving abroad for a long time, but I couldn’t get a Czech work visa during the COVID restrictions. I have a friend there who would have hired me. Then the war began, and the Czech Republic stopped issuing work visas altogether. I didn’t have enough money to leave without a destination or a plan, and I became depressed.
Then a distant relative died, and I learned that I was the heir. I sold the apartment I inherited, so now I can afford to leave.
I’ve been preparing for the move for almost a year. At first, I considered Germany because my grandfather had German roots. But that didn’t work out. It turned out my crafty grandfather had forged some documents in 1940 and had himself registered as Jewish, though his old photos suggest he would have looked right at home on a poster for some German political party. As a young man, he was a blond, athletic guy who stood nearly 6 feet 3 inches tall. How he managed to make a deal with the women at the passport office is a mystery.
In short, there’s no way to prove that I have German roots, so my wife and I decided to go to Paraguay. I think South America may be even better: taxes are lower than in Germany, and the culture makes more sense to me. We’ll fly to Foz do Iguaçu in Brazil because more tickets are available and they’re cheaper, then take a bus to Paraguay. This route takes us not to the capital, Asunción, but to the industrial area around Hohenau, where it’s easier to find affordable housing and work in my field.
We’re in the home stretch now. I’m waiting for apostilles for my documents and struggling to learn Spanish, which isn’t easy at my age. I’ve already sold or given away everything I’m not taking with me.
For me, staying or leaving isn’t really a choice, because I don’t want to take part in war crimes. I have no reason to return to Russia from Paraguay — even at the coldest time of year, nighttime temperatures there only occasionally fall to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. And there are no Internet restrictions.
Ksenia
Moscow
I’m panicking — sheer panic. The last time I was under this much stress, my hands started trembling, and I experienced my first symptoms of borderline personality disorder. I spent a year and a half taking antidepressants and going to therapy to learn how to manage my mental health. Now overwhelming feelings of hopelessness and helplessness keep washing over me in waves. My partner and I are both medical professionals, which means we’re automatically liable for military service.
My instinct is to run and never look back. Every day, I’m afraid, I cry, and I track price changes and political developments. I can think of only one thing: “I just hope we make it out in time.” But getting our degrees recognized so we can work abroad and transporting our pets will make leaving more complicated.
I was already thinking about moving four years ago, but circumstances made it impossible at the time.
The last straw for me — ridiculous as it may sound — was an advertisement for the notorious Alabuga Polytechnic. I saw the children and heard what they were saying, and the hair on my arms literally stood on end. I’m afraid to live in a country where a generation with such ideas is growing up. I’m terrified that my children will have classmates, fellow university students, colleagues, and neighbors like that.
My husband and I decided that we want to move to Germany. It came out ahead on every criterion that matters to me, including how difficult it would be to achieve certain life goals there. I’ve never lived anywhere but Russia, though my sister emigrated in 2023. I’ve also traveled a lot, so I have some idea of what to expect. It’s going to be fucking hard. But hard is better than impossible.
We’re now learning German, getting our pets microchipped and vaccinated, and obtaining apostilles for our documents. I applied for a second passport and withdrew all the money from my savings accounts. I still haven’t exchanged my rubles or figured out how and where to flee if mobilization begins before we can complete all the necessary preparations.
I don’t plan to return to Russia. No matter what happens or who is in power, I no longer believe in this country. I don’t believe it is my homeland, and I don’t want it to be my future children’s homeland.
Stanislav
Kirov region
When I think about the possibility of mobilization, I’m horrified and afraid for my life. I know I don’t want to become a killer or a war criminal. That was how I felt in 2022, and my reaction hasn’t changed since.
I’ve never emigrated, but I’ve traveled extensively: I’ve visited 20 countries, including some in Latin America, Africa, and Southeast Asia. In May, after returning from Morocco, I finally realized that Russia would not improve as long as Putin remained in power. The deciding factors were the drones, burning oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses, communications restrictions, and idiotic, barbaric laws.
I sold my most valuable possession — my computer — and left for South Korea with 1,000 euros in my pocket. I’ve been here for a month. I may be undocumented now, but I’ll obtain refugee status later and try to stay for the long term. It’s safe here, and even ordinary factory workers earn good wages.
Dmitry
Moscow
I first heard rumors of mobilization in May or June and didn’t take them seriously. But that changed over time.
My employer was considerate enough to hire a military lawyer to advise my colleagues and me. His conclusion was that no one is safe from mobilization. I, for example, never served in the military, am not registered with a military enlistment office, and am over 30, but I’m still at risk. Afterward, my employer drew up guidelines on how we could protect ourselves from possible mobilization. Moving to another country is just one option.
I’m still not completely sure whether I’ll go. For now, it’s my Plan B. I only recently bought an apartment, and I’m still paying it off. That makes leaving more difficult, but if necessary, I’ll transfer it to my mother and go. Plan A is to enroll in a part-time master’s program. I’m studying for the entrance exams now, and I’ll find out by mid-September whether I’ve been accepted. This option guarantees me nothing — military enlistment officers could simply stop me in the subway, restrain me, and take me away. But enrollment in a master’s program would give a lawyer grounds to demand my release.
If the master’s program doesn’t work out, I’ll go to Armenia. Renting a place in Yerevan would be a little expensive for me, so I’ll head to a smaller city. All I need to be happy is Wi-Fi and a grocery store. I’ll live there for a month or two at first, then see how events unfold. If things go badly — multiple draft notices and criminal charges for evasion — I’ll apply for a digital nomad visa in Spain and move there. I’ve already arranged this with my employer.
I’ve prepared the essential documents: I had my degree apostilled and translated, and I obtained a second passport. I also have a foreign bank card. If I decide to leave, I won’t have much time. I’ll urgently need to transfer my apartment, draw up a general power of attorney, buy tickets, and book accommodations.
Ivan D.
St. Petersburg
I started thinking about moving abroad in February or March 2026, as the number of repressive laws kept growing. You would think that in an election year, the authorities would be trying to make themselves look good. I first heard what sounded like rumors of post-election mobilization in early spring, and I was somewhat skeptical. But I have even less trust in the current government. Perhaps the mobilization will be covert.
Whatever happens, I definitely don’t want to be in Russia watching it unfold. Over time, my friends and I became increasingly certain that we would emigrate. None of us had ever emigrated before.
We’ll go to Georgia first because we can stay there for a long time without dealing with much paperwork. From there, we plan to apply for the United Kingdom’s Global Talent visa, since all of us have accomplishments that could qualify us. Those whose applications are rejected will decide what to do next, but we already have several backup options in mind.
I have almost everything ready for departure. My belongings are packed, my apartment is ready to rent out, my documents have been apostilled, and powers of attorney have been drawn up. The tickets and accommodations are booked. I’m gradually converting my rubles into cash and dollar-pegged cryptocurrency.
Leonid
Moscow
As a reserve officer, I have feared mobilization since the war began. At times, that fear has intensified or subsided. By this spring, after assessing the situation, I realized that I probably couldn’t put off deciding whether to emigrate any longer. And mobilization aside, other reasons to move have accumulated — the worsening socioeconomic situation, for example.
I moved to a Central Asian country that I had visited many times for work and vacations. My family hasn’t joined me yet; I’m here with my business partner. We’re developing a platform. My older child will arrive a little later. My wife and I decided that our younger child would finish ninth grade in Russia, after which the two of them would move here as well.
Alexey (name changed)
St. Petersburg
At first, the rumors of possible mobilization seemed baseless. Now I think there’s a fairly high chance that mobilization will happen in some form.
I’ve been thinking about emigrating for a long time, and now everything has come together — both my personal resources and the external threats. I’m turning 30 soon. I’ve only just begun building a family, and I need stability if I’m going to think about having children, for example. I don’t feel that stability in Russia, with its “horror without end.” One reason I’m determined to leave is the simple realization that, if I put in a great deal of effort, emigration offers me a chance to build a normal future. Russia offers no such chance and is unlikely to do so in the future.
I hadn’t emigrated before because I lacked the necessary resources, both financial and emotional.
I left for Serbia in late August, and I see it as a base for the next one to three years. I’m now applying for a residence permit. After that, I’ll see what happens in the world. I don’t plan to settle in Serbia for the rest of my life.
Georgy
Domodedovo, Moscow region
I’m 27 years old. I was born in Domodedovo and have lived here all my life.
Like many people, I think, I gradually began to feel that something bad — a new wave of mobilization — was coming. That feeling probably began in the fall of 2025, when advances on the front began slowing down and the economy noticeably deteriorated. News channels, political bloggers, and experts all began voicing the same concern.
That same fall, I began mentally preparing for the possibility of leaving, just in case. I made the final decision when drones began regularly attacking Moscow and the surrounding region. I saw them above my house. One morning, after explosions had kept me awake all night, I was on my way to work when I looked out from an overpass and saw thick columns of black smoke on the horizon. Wildberries warehouses were burning. That was when I decided I’d had enough and began making concrete preparations to leave. Before that, I had only traveled abroad.
I did everything I could. I built up an emergency fund, bought a powerful laptop, persuaded my employer to let me work remotely, obtained a second passport and apostilles for my documents, and renewed documents that were about to expire.
I’m in Yerevan now. I have friends here, so I’m not alone. I don’t have any firm plans. Preparing to leave and the move itself took an enormous amount out of me. First, I want to get settled here, regain some stability, improve my English, and either find a job abroad or try to start my own business.
Anton
Rostov-on-Don
I wanted to leave even before the war, but something always held me back: prices, a well-paid job with a European company, taxes, my parents, and other relatives.
For a very long time, I told myself that the war would end and then we would start living normally again. At the same time, I couldn’t believe that the country I remembered from before the war had really sunk this low. Russia was never perfect, but it felt as though it was developing, as though you could build something and move forward with the rest of the world.
My wife and I used to travel three or four times a year, and even in 2024 and 2025, returning to Russia felt normal. But after two trips in 2026, coming back became enormously stressful. It felt as though the rest of the world was simply getting on with life. Yes, there are crises, high prices, corruption, and employment problems everywhere, but at least those are ordinary problems people face in life.
The country isn’t merely developing more slowly than the rest of the world — it’s actually moving backward. Instead of wondering what new opportunities will appear in a few years, you wonder which of the things you’re used to will stop working next. For people in IT, this is a particular problem. I don’t even want to complain about VPNs anymore — everyone already knows what’s happening to them. And I don’t need a VPN to look at cat pictures; I need it to do my job properly.
It used to seem as though propaganda existed in a separate sphere and that the people around you understood what was really happening. It doesn’t feel that way anymore.
I have friends from Moscow who work in IT. Some used to work for American companies and were very close to Western culture. Now some of them say, “If you’re not with us, you’re against us. If you don’t like something, leave. If you voice criticism, you’re helping the enemy.” Some now seriously argue that it’s long past time to nuke Kyiv. But overall, the war doesn’t bother them. They go to bars and fly to Turkey and Thailand. One of them came to Taganrog, spent some time living with air-raid sirens and explosions, and decided that Ukraine needed to be bombed even harder.
For the first time, I now realize that even if the war ends tomorrow, almost nothing will return to how it was. The Internet restrictions will remain, international companies are unlikely to resume operations en masse, and militarization isn’t going anywhere — it will probably only intensify. People will return from the war after living for a long time in a completely different reality, accustomed to violence and large payments. I have no idea how they’ll return to ordinary life or where they’ll be able to earn that kind of money.
That is probably the main turning point for me: I used to be afraid that I would leave and then regret it, but now my greatest fear is that I won’t get out in time. The worst part isn’t even mobilization, the crisis, or any specific threat. It’s the feeling that you have become a stranger in your own country and that it’s moving in a completely different direction from where you want to go.
That’s why my wife and I are gathering the documents we need to move to Spain. Applying for residence permits and completing the other formalities will take quite a while, so we expect to move after New Year’s. I hope nothing happens this fall.
Pavel
St. Petersburg
The rumors of possible mobilization don’t surprise me at all. I feel only the grim certainty that people in this country are treated as worthless: when the authorities need cannon fodder, they get it. Human life is the highest value to me, so the authorities and I are going our separate ways. I don’t want to kill people. When did we incur such a debt to this country, and what for?
I have emigrated before, but only for four months, when I lived in Turkey. I don’t want to move until I have all my documents. But if the situation begins changing quickly, I’ll try to get a five-year passport on short notice, just so I can leave and sort everything out once I’m abroad.
I’ve already had my degrees apostilled, applied for a new passport and driver’s license after mine unexpectedly went “missing under unknown circumstances,” drawn up a general power of attorney for people close to me, and requested a criminal record certificate.
I’m not even considering any CIS country. I’m thinking more about Vietnam as an initial destination. After that, I may move to Indonesia, where Russian banks’ UnionPay cards work perfectly, and it is easier to obtain legal residency than in many other countries. Then I’ll consider a permanent move to Australia. But everything will depend on the situation in Russia — I may return.
Fyodor (name changed)
Kazan
I’m not seriously considering moving to another country right now, barring extreme scenarios such as a hybrid or full-scale civil war in Russia, a revolution involving mass violence, famine, or the complete collapse of the ruble.
I have emigrated before — I lived in Israel for almost two years. I didn’t like it at all, though not because it was expensive. My wife and I had money then and still do. There were other reasons.
Even so, I’m prepared. My new passport is almost ready, and I have the necessary money, apostilled documents, packed suitcases, and a clear plan of action.
One thing I know for certain is that I’m unhappy with the way European Union authorities treat Russians. For example, I was outraged by the European Court of Human Rights’ recent refusal to consider complaints from Russians.
I do, however, like the Armenian government’s approach: it is guided by practical considerations, not ideologically charged narratives. [If we move there,] my wife will be able to find a skilled job in Armenia, while I plan to work remotely.
But the move wouldn’t be long-term. I love Russia very much, value the history of Russia’s democratic movements, and remember times and events when it seemed that our beautiful future Russia was just around the corner — if only we pushed a little harder.
I’m not going to give up. Nor do I believe that my generation, born in the 1990s, has lost or that we will never again have a historic opportunity to fix Russia.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Suspect in Leipzig airport sabotage reportedly linked to Russian military intelligence
articles.body:
German investigators have identified two suspects in the sabotage attempt at Leipzig/Halle Airport, where a drone fitted with a detonator was found near a Ukrainian transport aircraft in early August. The suspects are Russian national Oleg L. and Belarusian national Andrei K., according to a report by German newspaper Welt am Sonntag. One of them, Oleg L., has ties to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, and was responsible for preparing the operation and handling its logistics.
German law enforcement officials investigating the attempted attack traced the operation to Russia’s GRU, with Welt am Sonntag citing investigative files obtained by the newspaper. Those materials indicate that Oleg L. appears to have overseen preparations and logistics for the operation. German security agencies believe he is a GRU officer.
The newspaper said Oleg L. entered Germany from Turkey through Berlin Brandenburg Airport. He later left the country from the same airport, flying to Serbia. Investigators believe he is now in Russia.
Welt am Sonntag also reported that German security agencies already knew of Oleg L.’s possible ties to Russian military intelligence when he entered the country, but did not place him under surveillance.
The suspected perpetrators planned to use three drones in the Leipzig airport sabotage operation. Two were destroyed during takeoff, while the third reached the Ukrainian aircraft. Investigators believe an explosion was avoided only because the detonator failed to function.
The second suspect is Belarusian national Andrei K. His DNA was found on an antenna that was used to control the drones. The DNA matched records in Finnish and Lithuanian police databases.
In Finland, he had been suspected of theft. He is also suspected of setting fire to a hardware store in the Polish city of Łódź in 2024.
The German publication Bild previously reported that a DNA trace found during the investigation of the Leipzig airport attack case matched DNA evidence from a 2024 arson attack on a DHL logistics center in Leipzig. The newspaper did not say whose DNA was found.
On Sept. 1, the German government formally accused Russia of carrying out a hybrid attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, where a drone with a detonator had been found near a Ukrainian transport plane on Aug. 5. At a news conference, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany would respond by closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and Russia’s consulate general in Bonn.
Russia, in turn, withdrew its consent for Germany’s consulate general in St. Petersburg to operate and shut down the country’s Goethe-Institut cultural centers nationwide.

articles.title: Civilians bear the brunt, with deadly US strikes in Iran and thousands displaced in Yemen
articles.body:
Civilians bear the brunt, with deadly US strikes in Iran and thousands displaced in Yemen
Independent UN human rights investigators called for an immediate cessation of hostilities on Monday following a series of United States airstrikes on Iran in recent weeks that have killed civilians as tensions ripple through the region.
“These strikes are yet another devastating reminder of the human cost of the conflict between the United States and Israel and Iran,” said Sara Hossain, chair of the Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Iran.
Civilian deaths have been recorded since the first days of the US-Israeli attacks in February, including strikes on a school that killed over 160 children.
“Civilians must be protected at all times, and constant care must be taken to spare civilians and civilians objects from the effect of hostilities,” she said.
Possible war crimes
Despite insisting that its military was not targeting civilians, US strikes hit a residential home on 30 July and a wedding celebration on 1 September, killing and injuring families, including women and children from marginalised minority communities, according to credible reports obtained by the mission.
Mission member Max du Plessis said “repeated airstrikes causing civilian casualties raise serious questions about whether all necessary measures are being taken to comply with States’ obligations under international law, including to take all precautionary measures to avoid civilian deaths.”
The mission urged all parties to the ongoing regional conflict to abide strictly by international law and cease hostilities, stressing that failure to do so may give rise to international responsibility, including for war crimes.
Calls for diplomacy, de-escalation
The mission stressed the vital importance of full and unfettered access for independent human rights monitors, journalists and investigators, including to secure critical evidence for the purposes of accountability.
The Human Rights Council-appointed investigators also reiterated their call for Member States to take immediate diplomatic action to halt the military conflict, de-escalate tensions and resume a credible, good faith dialogue on peace, human rights, justice and equal participation in political and public affairs.
The council established the fact-finding mission in 2022 to investigate alleged violations in Iran related to the protests and extended on 23 January 2026 for two years.
Learn more about the mission here.
Fighting displaces thousands in Yemen
At least 80,000 people were displaced by escalating fighting in Yemen in recent days, many forced to flee for the second or third time, according to the UN refugee agency, UNHCR.
“Civilians must be protected,” UNHCR said in a social media post. “Humanitarian aid must reach those in need.”
Millions in Yemen already need urgent assistance, but ongoing fighting between the Saudi-backed authorities and Iran-backed Houthi militia have recently escalated.
Media reports indicate that Houthis fighters have seized multiple islands in the Red Sea and a crucial Yemeni port city, giving them greater control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, where they have been attacking Saudi shipping.
Deteriorating conditions
Meanwhile, conditions on the ground are worsening, the UN migration agency, IOM, warned over the weekend.
“The situation in Yemen is deteriorating quickly,” IOM country director Abdusattor Esoev told UN News last Friday, adding that the agency is monitoring the situation and responding to urgent humanitarian needs.
Listen to the full interview here:
Despite extremely difficult operating conditions, humanitarian efforts continue to provide urgent aid, from food to shelter, according to the UN emergency relief agency, OCHA.
As of 12 September, they have provided aid to thousands of households, however supplies are critically low, and funding is falling short of needs, OCHA warned, emphasising that humanitarian access and movements remain severely constrained due to insecurity, with suspended operations in several locations on Yemen’s west coast alongside impassable or restricted access to key roads.
‘Toll on civilians is increasing’
At least 18,000 households – or 125,000 people – have been displaced since the start of the month, according to the latest OCHA updates.
“The toll on civilians is increasing,” UN Deputy Spokesperson Farhan Haq said.
Between 1 September and Monday, the UN human rights office, OHCHR, has verified 40 civilian casualties – eight people killed and 32 others injured. Women and children account for half of those killed and more than half of those injured.
“OCHA once again calls on all parties to protect civilians, respect international humanitarian law and facilitate safe and unimpeded humanitarian access so that urgently needed assistance can reach communities in need,” Mr. Haq said.

articles.title: Houthis claim drone, missile strikes on airbase in Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
DOHA, September 14. /TASS/. Yemen’s Ansar Allah (Houthi) rebel movement claims to have conducted a series of ballistic missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid Air Base in the city of Khamis Mushait.
"Yemen’s Armed Forces carried out a large-scale operation against military and infrastructure facilities, including aircraft hangars, runways, ammunition depots and other targets at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait," Houthi military Spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on Telegram. He added that the attack involved "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones."
The situation in Yemen escalated sharply in early September when the rebel movement launched an offensive in the country’s southwest. At the same time, it began carrying out missile and drone strikes on Red Sea coastal areas and the outskirts of the city of Taiz, seeking to sever access routes to the port of Mocha and advance toward areas along the strategic Bab-el-Mandeb Strait.
On September 11, the Houthi military spokesperson announced that Ansar Allah units had begun an operation on Yemen’s west coast to push back Saudi forces. According to him, the operation was due to "attacks on civilians, villages and areas on the west coast by Saudi-backed forces, which have been going on for several years." Ansar Allah Political Bureau member Hizam al-Asad confirmed to TASS on September 12 that the Houthis had concluded an operation to take control of areas in western Yemen adjacent to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

articles.title: No NATO army has fought modern war: Ukrainian officers set their battlefield practice against NATO doctrine and exposed where its assumptions no longer fit
articles.body:
NATO officers are now learning from Ukraine’s combat experience in UAVs, electronic warfare, and intelligence. Ukrainian military personnel have held a series of seminars for officers from the Polish and German armies on applying lessons from modern warfare to military command and decision-making, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said.
No NATO army has fought a modern war. Because Ukraine's soldiers are the only ones with years of combat under saturating drones and jamming, their experience is now reshaping how the alliance plans and trains, not the reverse.
The seminars have mixed theory with live exercises and set Ukrainian operational practice against NATO's written doctrine, exposing where the alliance's assumptions about maneuver, command, and the use of force no longer fit a battlefield run by technology.
Ukraine teaches the lessons of drone war
"Ukrainian officers bring the experience of real modern war, and the practical work lets us test together how it can be used to train troops," said Colonel Valerii Vyshnivskyi.
He is Ukraine's senior representative at the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center (JATEC), the first joint civil-military institution between NATO and Ukraine.
The course runs through a joint centre
The three-week event took place in Lublin, at the base of the Lithuanian-Polish-Ukrainian Brigade, which provided the facilities. It was part of JATEC's support for a program called Captains' Training, intended to facilitate the exchange of tactical-level lessons between Ukraine's forces and NATO. The officers worked through Troop Leading Procedures for planning a company's actions and the Military Decision Making Process, used by a battalion staff.
In Ukraine, the Come Back Alive foundation has backed the same course since 2022.

							“We expect specifics from our partners”: Zelenskyy says Ukraine will accept energy truce with Russia only if West guarantees Moscow won’t break it after its elections
